Impression: Asymmetric hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with dynamic LVOT obstruction and patchy myocardial fibrosis at the RV insertion points.

Brain MRI demonstrates a 2.5 x 2.0 cm focal intraparenchymal lesion within the left basal ganglia/internal capsule region. The mass displays mixed signal intensity, with a hypointense rim on T2-weighted and susceptibility-weighted imaging, corresponding to subacute hematoma containing extracellular methemoglobin. Significant surrounding vasogenic edema and mild compression of the left lateral ventricle are present.

Impression: Subacute intraparenchymal hemorrhage within the left basal ganglia/internal capsule, typical for hypertensive etiology. Mild local mass effect without significant midline shift.

Fetal MRI at 32 weeks 5 days gestation. High-resolution multiplanar sequences demonstrate herniation of the stomach and multiple small bowel loops into the left chest cavity. There is severe rightward mediastinal shift with compression of the fetal heart. The left lung is hypoplastic, with a calculated lung volume below the 5th percentile for gestational age. Fetal brain development and sulcation are normal, and ventricular atria measure 6.4 mm.

Polyhydramnios is present. Impression: Left congenital diaphragmatic hernia with severe ipsilateral pulmonary hypoplasia and mediastinal shift. Prognostic assessment suggests high risk of neonatal respiratory distress.

Brain MRI demonstrates a large, heterogeneous, ring-enhancing mass centered within the right frontoparietal lobe, measuring 4.5 x 3.8 x 3.6 cm. The lesion features a necrotic core, thick irregular peripheral enhancement, and substantial surrounding vasogenic edema causing a 7 mm leftward midline shift. Compression of the right lateral ventricle is noted.

Impression: Large, necrotic, ring-enhancing right frontoparietal mass, highly characteristic of a high-grade glioma (such as glioblastoma multiforme) or less likely a solitary metastasis. Neurosurgical consultation is urgently requested.

Fetal MRI at 36 weeks gestation demonstrates advanced gyral development. Multiple secondary and tertiary sulci are clearly defined throughout both cerebral hemispheres, indicating normal cortical maturation matching late-third-trimester gestation. The ventricular atria measure 6.4 mm on the left and 6.2 mm on the right, well within normal limits. Subarachnoid spaces and CSF spaces are appropriate.

The fetal thoracic, abdominal, and musculoskeletal structures show no focal lesions or anomalies. Normal cardiac position and amniotic fluid volume. Impression: Normal fetal brain and visceral development at 36 weeks gestation.

Cardiac MRI evaluates severe aortic stenosis. The aortic valve is calcified and trileaflet with restricted mobility. Planimetry reveals a valve area of 0.8 cm2 and phase-contrast velocity mapping demonstrates a peak velocity of 4.2 m/s across the valve. Significant concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is present (mass index 112 g/m2), with a normal cavity size. LVEF is calculated at 50%.

Impression: Severe calcific aortic stenosis with associated concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and borderline-preserved left ventricular systolic function. No significant myocardial fibrosis identified.

MR imaging of the brain was performed utilizing multiplanar, multisequence protocols. The brain parenchyma shows normal signal intensity throughout. There is no evidence of intracranial mass lesion, acute ischemia, hemorrhage, or demyelinating plaques. The ventricles and sulci are within normal limits for patient age.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. No structural, ischemic, or inflammatory abnormalities identified to explain the patient's complaints of postpartum headaches.

Cardiac MRI was ordered to evaluate for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). The right ventricle is severely dilated (RVEDVI of 135 mL/m²) with regional dyskinesis and microaneurysm formation within the right ventricular outflow tract and inferior wall. High-resolution T1-weighted imaging reveals intramyocardial fat infiltration in the RV free wall. Right ventricular ejection fraction is depressed at 34%, while left ventricular size and function remain normal (LVEF 58%).

Impression: Structural features strongly characteristic of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting major task force criteria. Clinical correlation with ECG findings and genetic testing is suggested.

Fetal brain MRI at 26 weeks gestation reveals an enlarged cisterna magna measuring 12.5 mm in the anteroposterior diameter. The cerebellar vermis is fully formed, of normal size, and is not rotated superiorly. There is no communication between the posterior fossa fluid space and the fourth ventricle. Symmetrical lateral ventricles measure 6.2 mm at the atria. Sulcation patterns are normal for 26 weeks.

No other CNS or systemic abnormalities are identified. Impression: Isolated megacisterna magna (Dandy-Walker variant). This is typically a benign variation given the intact cerebellar vermis.

Cardiac MRI evaluates atypical chest pain in a 42-year-old female. Evaluation of cardiac structure and function demonstrates normal left ventricular cavity dimensions and normal wall thickness. Left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 60% with symmetric wall motion. The right ventricle is likewise of normal size and exhibits preserved systolic function (EF 55%).

No areas of abnormal signal intensity are seen on T2-weighted or T1-weighted mapping sequences. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging demonstrates no focal scarring, replacement fibrosis, or inflammatory change. Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI study. No evidence of ischemia, infarction, myocarditis, or structural cardiomyopathy.

Brain MRI with dedicated orbital sequences demonstrates flattening of the posterior sclera bilaterally, along with distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space and mild tortuosity of the optic nerves. There is also partial empty sella syndrome noted. The parenchymal signal intensity is otherwise normal, and no mass lesion is identified.

Impression: Neuroimaging findings of intracranial hypertension, consistent with Pseudotumor Cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension). Correlate clinically with ophthalmologic exam findings.

MRI angiogram of the thoracic aorta demonstrates a focal, hemodynamically significant narrowing of the aortic isthmus just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, measuring 8 mm in internal diameter. There is prominent dilatation of the internal mammary and intercostal arteries, representing extensive collateral pathways. Moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is noted secondary to the obstruction, with an LVEF of 62%.

Impression: Significant maternal coarctation of the aorta with associated collateral vascularization and concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Close perinatal monitoring is advised.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate atypical chest pain and palpitations in a 45-year-old female. Cine imaging demonstrates normal cardiac chambers with appropriate myocardial thickness. Left ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes are within normal physiological limits. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is calculated at 64% with normal, symmetric wall motion and no regional hypokinesis. Right ventricular size and systolic function are also normal with an ejection fraction of 58%. T2-weighted and T1-mapping sequences show no evidence of myocardial edema, inflammation, or infiltration. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging demonstrates no myocardial scar, fibrosis, or focal enhancement in either ventricle. Valvular structures are morphologically normal with no hemodynamically significant regurgitation or stenosis.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI with preserved biventricular systolic function, normal chamber dimensions, and no evidence of myocardial scar, edema, or late gadolinium enhancement. No structural etiology is identified to account for the patient's palpitations.

Cardiac MRI was performed for the assessment of recurrent palpitations and chest discomfort. Multiplanar cine imaging shows normal left ventricular size and systolic function with an ejection fraction of 63%. Right ventricular volumes, wall motion, and systolic function are likewise normal (EF 56%). There is no evidence of focal myocardial edema on T2-weighted STIR images, and myocardial perfusion during first-pass imaging is homogeneous. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) sequences show no abnormal myocardial enhancement to suggest focal scar or replacement fibrosis.

Impression: Structurally normal cardiac MRI with preserved biventricular function and no evidence of myocardial scar or active inflammation. No imaging features to suggest a structural etiology for the patient's symptoms.

MRI of the brain demonstrates a ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe measuring 2.1 x 1.8 cm. The central cavity shows restricted diffusion on DWI with corresponding low ADC values, indicative of purulent fluid. Prominent surrounding vasogenic edema is present, causing local mass effect and compression of the left frontal horn.

Impression: Left frontal lobe ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion, highly characteristic of a brain abscess. Urgent neurosurgical and infectious disease consultation is recommended.

High-resolution MR angiography of the thoracic aorta reveals a discrete narrowing of the aortic arch distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, measuring only 8 mm in diameter. Pronounced collateral vessels, including dilated internal mammary and intercostal arteries, are visualized. Left ventricular hypertrophy is noted secondary to chronic pressure overload.

Impression: Severe discrete coarctation of the thoracic aorta with prominent collateral circulation and secondary left ventricular hypertrophy.

Brain MR imaging reveals a large, heterogeneous, thick-walled ring-enhancing mass in the right temporal lobe measuring 4.2 x 3.8 x 3.5 cm. Extensive surrounding vasogenic edema is present, causing significant compression of the right lateral ventricle and 6 mm of leftward midline shift. Central necrosis and focal hemorrhagic products are noted within the cavity.

Impression: Large necrotic ring-enhancing mass in the right temporal lobe, highly suspicious for glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) or solitary metastasis. Urgent neurosurgical evaluation is indicated.

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks gestation demonstrates a partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. High-resolution sagittal sequences show that only the anterior portions (rostrum and body) of the corpus callosum are present, with complete absence of the splenium. This is associated with mild colpocephaly, with the posterior horns of the lateral ventricles measuring 10.8 mm. Cortical sulcation is age-appropriate.

The optic chiasm and pituitary gland appear normal. No extracranial abnormalities are seen. Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated mild posterior ventriculomegaly.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation reveals a large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The stomach, multiple loops of small bowel, and a portion of the left lobe of the liver have herniated into the left hemithorax, causing a significant rightward mediastinal shift and severe compression of the contralateral lung. The fetal brain shows normal morphology and age-appropriate sulculation.

The lateral ventricular atria measure 6.1 mm, and no intracranial anomalies are detected. Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic herniation of abdominal organs and significant mediastinal shift. Associated pulmonary hypoplasia is suspected.

Cardiac MRI utilizing pharmacological stress perfusion and tissue viability protocols. There are no regional perfusion abnormalities during peak vasodilator stress. Left and right ventricular chamber dimensions and wall thicknesses are normal. The biventricular ejection fractions are normal (LVEF 62%, RVEF 55%). No evidence of late gadolinium enhancement or interstitial fibrosis is demonstrated on myocardial tissue characterization.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. There is no evidence of stress-induced myocardial ischemia, prior myocardial infarction, or macrovascular coronary artery disease.

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks 4 days gestation demonstrates features of a severe skeletal dysplasia, highly consistent with Thanatophoric Dysplasia. There is marked, severe shortening of all long bones (rhizomelic micromelia) with characteristic bowing of the femora ('telephone receiver' appearance). The thorax is extremely narrow and bell-shaped with short ribs, leading to severe secondary pulmonary hypoplasia. The fetal head is disproportionately large with frontal bossing, but intracranial anatomy and sulcation are normal for 27 weeks. Lateral ventricular atria measure 7.1 mm.

The fetal spine shows flattened vertebral bodies (platyspondyly) but remains aligned. Polyhydramnios is noted. Impression: Severe skeletal dysplasia with features characteristic of Thanatophoric Dysplasia, associated with narrow thorax, severe pulmonary hypoplasia, and polyhydramnios.

MR imaging of the brain was obtained in this postpartum patient presenting with severe headache and visual disturbances. There is bilateral, symmetric patchy T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the subcortical white matter of the occipital and parietal lobes, with no evidence of restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC sequences. No acute intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect is identified.

Impression: Findings are highly characteristic of Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) in the setting of postpartum preeclampsia. Recommend clinical correlation and blood pressure monitoring; these changes are typically reversible with appropriate management.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation demonstrates completely normal structural fetal development. Cortical sulcation and gyration are well-developed and appropriate for the third trimester. The lateral ventricles are symmetric, with the atria measuring 6.1 mm on the left and 5.9 mm on the right. The corpus callosum and posterior fossa are unremarkable.

The chest, abdomen, spine, and fetal extremities are completely normal. Amniotic fluid volume is normal. Impression: Normal fetal MRI with normal intracranial development and no structural anomalies identified.

MRI of the heart shows normal cardiac chamber dimensions and wall thicknesses. The left ventricular ejection fraction is 62% and the right ventricular ejection fraction is 59%. There are no segmental wall motion abnormalities or areas of delayed myocardial wash-out. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging shows no abnormal focal signal in either ventricle.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. There is no evidence of structural heart disease, focal fibrosis, or myocardial dysfunction.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrates normal anatomical structure. The cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres are symmetric, and the ventricular system is unremarkable. There is no evidence of acute ischemia, hemorrhage, mass lesion, or abnormal enhancement. The internal auditory canals are symmetric and normal in appearance.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals. No structural cause found to explain the patient's symptoms of dizziness and episodic syncope.

Fetal MRI at 33 weeks gestation reveals severe bilateral lateral ventriculomegaly. The left atrial width measures 18.2 mm and the right measures 17.9 mm. There is thinning of the cerebral parenchyma and dilation of the third ventricle. The fourth ventricle is normal in size, characteristic of congenital aqueductal stenosis. Cortical sulcation is appropriate for 33 weeks.

No spinal anomalies are observed. Impression: Severe bilateral ventriculomegaly, highly suggestive of congenital aqueductal stenosis.

Brain MRI demonstrates herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 7 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. The tonsils are pointed in morphology. There is associated effacement of the CSF space at the craniocervical junction. The cervical spinal cord was evaluated to the level of C3, showing no evidence of a syrinx.

Impression: Chiari I malformation with 7 mm tonsillar ectopia. No associated syringomyelia is visualized in the upper cervical cord.

Brain MRI demonstrates symmetric areas of high T2/FLAIR signal intensity in the subcortical white matter of the bilateral parietal and occipital lobes. There is no associated diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC, which is characteristic of vasogenic edema. These findings occur in the setting of severe postpartum preeclampsia.

Impression: Bilateral parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR hyperintensities consistent with Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES). Findings correlate with the clinical diagnosis of severe preeclampsia.

Brain MRI shows a large, dural-based, intensely and homogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass along the right parasagittal parietal convexity, measuring 3.5 x 3.2 x 2.8 cm. The mass exerts local mass effect on the adjacent postcentral gyrus, with a thin CSF cleft and prominent 'dural tail' sign. Surrounding vasogenic edema in the white matter is mild to moderate.

Impression: Right parasagittal parietal extra-axial lesion, most consistent with a benign meningioma. Neurosurgical follow-up is recommended to discuss monitoring versus resection.

MR venogram and brain MRI demonstrate an absence of normal flow void and a loss of contrast enhancement within the posterior superior sagittal sinus and the right transverse sinus. A focal hyperintensity on T1-weighted imaging suggests acute thrombus. There is mild localized cortical swelling in the right parietal lobe without signs of hemorrhagic venous infarction.

Impression: Acute dural venous sinus thrombosis involving the posterior superior sagittal and right transverse sinuses. This is a recognized postpartum risk factor; close clinical monitoring for signs of venous infarct is advised.

Cardiac MRI was performed for preconception counseling in a patient with a strong family history of dilated cardiomyopathy. Multiplanar cine imaging demonstrates completely normal left and right ventricular volumes, wall thickness, and systolic function. LVEF is 63% and RVEF is 58%. There is no late gadolinium enhancement to suggest focal fibrosis.

Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI. No structural, functional, or tissue characterization abnormalities are present to suggest familial cardiomyopathy.

Cardiac MRI shows mild left ventricular dilation with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) reduced at 51%. T2-weighted triple IR sequences demonstrate patchy areas of high signal intensity primarily in the mid-myocardial layer of the lateral and inferolateral free walls, consistent with acute myocardial edema. Parametric T2 mapping confirms elevated relaxation times peaking at 62 ms in these regions.

Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging reveals non-ischemic, patchy mid-wall to subepicardial enhancement within the basal and mid-ventricular lateral walls. Impression: Findings meet the updated Lake Louise Criteria for acute myocarditis, demonstrating myocardial edema and non-ischemic myocardial injury (LGE) in a pattern suggestive of post-viral etiology.

Cardiac MRI shows a regional wall motion abnormality in the LAD territory, with akinesis of the mid-to-apical anterior wall and septum. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging reveals a subendocardial hyperenhancement involving approximately 30-40% of the wall thickness in these regions, confirming a subendocardial myocardial infarction. The global left ventricular ejection fraction is reduced at 44%.

Impression: Ischemic heart disease with subendocardial myocardial infarction in the LAD distribution. Viability is preserved in the affected segments given the subendocardial nature of the enhancement.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate for residual scar following an episode of myocarditis 6 months ago. Active myocardial edema is no longer present on T2-weighted sequencing. The left ventricular volumes and overall systolic function have recovered, with a current LVEF of 58% (previously 45%).

However, persistent mid-wall and subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) remains visible in the basal inferolateral wall, indicating mature focal scar tissue. Impression: Resolved active myocarditis with a persistent, non-ischemic subepicardial scar in the inferolateral wall; ventricular function has normalized.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates a Dandy-Walker variant. There is a prominent, fluid-filled cisterna magna measuring 13.0 mm in the anteroposterior dimension, associated with a mild defect of the inferior cerebellar vermis. The superior vermis is intact, and the cerebellar hemispheres appear normal. The ventricular system is mildly dilated, with the lateral ventricular atrium measuring 8.5 mm.

The sulcation patterns are completely appropriate for 29 weeks. Extracranial anatomy is unremarkable. Impression: Dandy-Walker variant characterized by a prominent cisterna magna and mild inferior vermian deficiency, with mild associated ventriculomegaly.

Fetal MRI performed at 30 weeks gestation. Cerebral cortical maturation shows appropriate secondary sulcus formation. The lateral ventricular atria are symmetric and measure 6.3 mm. The corpus callosum is completely visualized and normal. Cerebellar hemispheres and vermis are normal in morphology and size.

Fetal thoracic, abdominal, and spinal structures are unremarkable. Placenta and amniotic fluid volume are normal. Impression: Normal fetal MRI showing appropriate structural brain development and no evidence of fetal anomalies.

A well-circumscribed, extra-axial, dural-based mass is noted along the olfactory groove/anterior cranial fossa, measuring approximately 3.2 x 2.8 x 2.5 cm. The lesion is homogeneously hyperintense to gray matter on T2-weighted sequences and demonstrates intense, uniform enhancement following gadolinium administration, with a prominent "dural tail" sign. Moderate surrounding vasogenic edema is present in the adjacent bilateral frontal lobes.

Impression: Olfactory groove extra-axial mass, classic for a benign meningioma. Associated mild mass effect on the frontal lobes is noted.

Fetal MRI at 30 weeks gestation evaluated for transient fetal arrhythmia. Intracranial structures demonstrate normal parenchymal signal intensity and morphology. The cerebral hemispheres exhibit appropriate operculization and sulcation progress for 30 weeks, including well-defined parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci. The lateral ventricular atria measure 6.1 mm on the left and 6.3 mm on the right. The corpus callosum and brainstem are completely intact, and the cerebellar vermis is normal in size and lobulation.

The fetal chest and abdomen are normal, and the spine is intact without dysraphism. Impression: Normal fetal brain MRI at 30 weeks gestation. No structural CNS abnormalities or signs of cortical migration disorders are present.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed utilizing multiplanar, multisequence protocols. There is no evidence of intra-axial or extra-axial mass lesion, acute ischemia, or intracranial hemorrhage. The ventricles and sulci are within normal limits for patient age, with no signs of hydrocephalus. The major intracranial vascular flow voids are well-preserved.

Visualized paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells are clear. Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. No structural, vascular, or acute pathological changes identified.

Cardiac MRI shows severe concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle with a septal thickness of 17 mm and a posterolateral wall thickness of 16 mm. Aortic valve leaflets are severely thickened and calcified with restricted excursion. Velocity-encoded MRI across the aortic valve demonstrates a peak velocity of 4.2 m/s, yielding a calculated peak aortic valve gradient of 70 mmHg and a mean gradient of 44 mmHg.

Impression: Severe valvular aortic stenosis with secondary concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Left ventricular systolic function is preserved with an ejection fraction of 61%.

Dedicated MR imaging of the sella turcica demonstrates a small, hypoenhancing focus measuring 5 x 4 mm within the left lateral wing of the anterior pituitary gland. The lesion is subtly hypointense on T1-weighted images and demonstrates delayed contrast uptake compared to the normal pituitary parenchyma. There is no evidence of suprasellar extension, optic chiasm compression, or cavernous sinus invasion. The infundibulum is midline.

Impression: Small left-sided pituitary microadenoma, measuring approximately 5 mm, without secondary mass effect on the optic apparatus. Correlation with serum prolactin and endocrine evaluation is advised.

Brain MR demonstrates multiple small, well-circumscribed cystic lesions located at the gray-white matter junction of both cerebral hemispheres, measuring 4-8 mm in size. Several of these lesions show a tiny eccentric nodule inside, representing the scolex, with minimal surrounding edema and mild ring-like contrast enhancement.

Impression: Multiple parenchymal brain lesions, highly characteristic of neurocysticercosis in the vesicular and colloidal vesicular stages.

Cardiac MRI reveals significant transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) affecting the apex, mid-anterior, and anteroseptal walls of the left ventricle. This pattern represents approximately 35% of total LV myocardial mass and is highly characteristic of a prior myocardial infarction in the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery distribution. The LVEF is reduced at 35%, with prominent akinesis of the infarcted segments.

Impression: Severe ischemic cardiomyopathy with a large transmural anteroseptal and apical myocardial infarction. Preserved viability is limited in the affected regions, indicating a chronic, non-viable scar.

Cardiac MRI reveals severe hypokinesis to akinesis of the apical and mid-ventricular segments of the left ventricle, with hyperkinesis of the basal segments, demonstrating classic 'apical ballooning.' The left ventricular ejection fraction is significantly depressed at 35%. The right ventricle is functionally normal with an ejection fraction of 52%.

No late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is identified in the hypocontractile segments, excluding acute myocardial infarction. Impression: Findings are highly characteristic of Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy, showing transient apical ballooning in the absence of coronary-pattern late gadolinium enhancement.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates completely normal structural anatomy. The fetal brain shows appropriate sulcation and gyration for 28 weeks, with expected progression of the calcarine and parieto-occipital fissures. The lateral ventricles measure 6.0 mm bilaterally. The posterior fossa, including cerebellum and cisterna magna, is completely normal.

Fetal heart, stomach, kidneys, and extremities are fully visualized and appear anatomically intact and age-appropriate. Impression: Unremarkable fetal MRI study demonstrating normal, age-appropriate structural and central nervous system development.

Fetal MRI performed at 24 weeks gestation demonstrates a classic Dandy-Walker malformation. There is severe hypoplasia and upward rotation of the cerebellar vermis. A large cystic space is noted in the posterior fossa, which directly communicates with the dilated fourth ventricle, causing elevation of the tentorium. The lateral ventricles are moderately dilated, with the atrium measuring 11.5 mm. Cortical sulcation is appropriate for 24 weeks gestation.

The corpus callosum is visible but thin. Remaining fetal organs appear within normal limits. Impression: Dandy-Walker malformation characterized by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, posterior fossa cyst, and mild ventriculomegaly. Prenatal pediatric neurology consultation is advised.

MRI demonstrates severe asymmetric septal hypertrophy, with the maximal diastolic wall thickness of the interventricular septum measuring 22 mm. Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve is present, resulting in dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and moderate mitral regurgitation. There is a hyperdynamic left ventricular state with an LVEF of 74%. Late gadolinium enhancement reveals patchy mid-wall fibrosis within the hypertrophied septal segments.

Impression: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with severe asymmetric septal hypertrophy, SAM of the mitral valve, dynamic LVOT obstruction, and localized myocardial fibrosis.

Fetal MRI at 32 weeks gestation reveals complete absence of the corpus callosum. The lateral ventricles demonstrate a classic "tear-drop" configuration (colpocephaly) with dilation of the occipital horns measuring 12.5 mm and narrowing of the frontal horns. Steer-horn appearance of the lateral ventricles is noted on coronal imaging. Probst bundles are visualized running parallel to the interhemispheric fissure. Cortical sulcation patterns show abnormal radial arrangement, pointing toward the third ventricle, which is dorsally displaced.

The posterior fossa, brainstem, and fetal somatic anatomy are otherwise normal. No other structural anomalies are seen. Impression: Complete agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated colpocephaly. No other intracranial or extracranial anomalies identified.

Brain MRI demonstrates bilateral, symmetric areas of high signal intensity on T2/FLAIR sequences located primarily in the subcortical white matter of the occipital and parietal lobes. These areas do not show restricted diffusion on DWI, indicating vasogenic rather than cytotoxic edema.

Impression: Radiographic findings consistent with Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES), clinically correlating with the patient's history of severe preeclampsia and eclamptic seizures during labor.

Brain MR imaging demonstrates normal parenchymal volume and signal characteristics throughout. The ventricles, basal cisterns, and subarachnoid spaces are normal in size and appearance for the patient's age. No signs of intracranial mass, acute ischemia, or vascular pathology are noted. Both internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles are completely clear.

Impression: Completely normal brain MRI. No structural abnormality or pathology found to explain the patient's persistent peripheral vertigo and dizziness.

Fetal MRI at 21 weeks gestation demonstrates complete absence of both fetal kidneys in the renal fossae. No renal tissue is identified in the pelvis or ectopic locations. Severe oligohydramnios/anhydramnios is present, causing extreme crowding of the fetal parts. The fetal urinary bladder is not visualized, consistent with lack of urine production.

The fetal lungs are severely compressed, with calculated lung volumes far below normal limits for gestational age. Intracranial structures show compression artifacts but no overt malformations. Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis associated with anhydramnios and severe pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence).

The brain parenchyma is normal in appearance with preserved grey-white matter differentiation. There are no areas of abnormal signal intensity on T1, T2, or FLAIR sequences. The ventricles and extra-axial spaces are normal in size and symmetric. No mass effect, midline shift, or acute ischemia is detected. The brainstem and cerebellum demonstrate normal morphology.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. No intracranial abnormality is seen to explain the patient's acute-onset dizziness and vertigo.

MR imaging of the brain was obtained following standard institutional protocols. The cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres demonstrate normal morphology and signal intensity. The ventricular system, sulci, and basal cisterns are completely symmetric and age-appropriate. There is no evidence of acute hemorrhage, territorial infarction, or abnormal enhancement.

Impression: Unremarkable magnetic resonance imaging of the brain. No structural, inflammatory, or vascular abnormalities are identified to explain the patient's complaints of vertigo.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation reveals partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior corpus callosum is present, but the rostrum, genu, and splenium are absent. There is associated mild ventriculomegaly, with the lateral ventricles displaying a teardrop configuration (colpocephaly) and the atrium measuring 10.5 mm on the left. The sulcal patterns are mildly distorted but intact.

All other fetal anatomical systems are normal. Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated mild colpocephaly. Postnatal MRI evaluation and developmental follow-up are recommended.

Brain MR focusing on the sella turcica demonstrates a well-circumscribed, enhancing mass arising from the adenohypophysis, measuring 1.8 x 1.5 x 1.6 cm. The mass extends superiorly into the suprasellar cistern, causing mild upward displacement and compression of the optic chiasm. There is no invasion into the bilateral cavernous sinuses, and the internal carotid arteries remain patent with normal flow voids.

Impression: Pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension and mild compression of the optic chiasm. Clinical correlation with visual field testing and endocrine panels is recommended.

Fetal MRI at 23 weeks gestation demonstrates severe oligohydramnios and complete bilateral renal agenesis. No normal renal parenchyma or renal arteries are identified within either renal fossa or within the pelvis. The fetal urinary bladder is not visualized, indicating a lack of urine production. Secondary severe pulmonary hypoplasia is suspected due to oligohydramnios and small thoracic volume.

The fetal brain demonstrates age-appropriate sulcation, and the lateral ventricular atria measure 7.1 mm. No obvious skeletal dysplasias or cardiac malformations are seen. Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis associated with severe oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia (classic Potter sequence). Prognosis is extremely poor.

Brain MRI performed for evaluation of acute-onset optic neuritis and sensory loss. There is a new, enhancing focal lesion within the posterior aspect of the left optic nerve. Multiple periventricular and subcortical white matter FLAIR hyperintensities are present, with two of the periventricular plaques demonstrating thick ring enhancement, indicating active inflammatory demyelination.

Impression: Active demyelinating disease consistent with a Multiple Sclerosis relapse. Multiple chronic lesions are present along with acutely enhancing active lesions including left optic neuritis.

Cardiac MRI shows severe dilation of the right ventricle with an end-diastolic volume index of 132 mL/m². There is regional right ventricular free wall dyskinesis, characterized by aneurysmal outpouching and microaneurysms in the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) and apex. The right ventricular ejection fraction is severely reduced at 34%.

Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging demonstrating patchy, transmural hyperenhancement within the thinned right ventricular free wall, indicative of fibrofatty replacement. Left ventricular size and function are preserved with an ejection fraction of 60%. Impression: Findings are highly consistent with Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting major Task Force criteria.

MRI of the brain reveals a well-defined, dural-based, extra-axial mass along the left parietal convexity. The lesion measures 2.2 x 2.0 x 1.9 cm, is isointense on T1 and T2 sequences, demonstrates intense uniform contrast enhancement, and exhibits a prominent 'dural tail' sign. There is minimal underlying vasogenic edema and no major compression of the regional cortex.

Impression: Left parietal convexity dural-based mass, highly characteristic of a benign meningioma. Recommended interval MRI surveillance in 6 months.

Fetal MR imaging at 22 weeks gestation reveals a midline occipital bone defect. There is herniation of a small meningeal sac containing cerebrospinal fluid and a small portion of occipital lobe brain parenchyma, indicating an occipital encephalocele. The lateral ventricles are mildly dilated with an atrium measuring 10.2 mm. Brain development is otherwise appropriate for 22 weeks with normal smooth cortical hemispheres and early opercularization.

All other spinal elements appear intact, and no other neural tube defects are identified. Visceral organs are normal. Impression: Occipital encephalocele associated with mild ventriculomegaly. Pediatric neurosurgery and prenatal maternal-fetal medicine follow-up is recommended.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates severe dilation of the left ventricle with an end-diastolic volume index of 128 mL/m2. Global left ventricular systolic function is severely reduced, with an ejection fraction of 24%. High-resolution late gadolinium enhancement sequences reveal a linear mid-myocardial stripe of enhancement in the basal-to-mid interventricular septum, typical of a non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. The right ventricle is also mildly dilated with a reduced ejection fraction of 42%.

Impression: Severe non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy with biventricular dysfunction (LVEF 24%) and a classic mid-myocardial enhancement pattern suggesting intrinsic myocardial fibrosis.

Brain MRI reveals mild generalized cortical atrophy and age-appropriate ventricular enlargement. There is no evidence of intracranial mass, acute ischemia, or hemorrhage. No abnormal parenchymal enhancement or restricted diffusion is seen.

Impression: Brain MRI demonstrating mild senescent cortical atrophy and chronic microvascular white matter changes, consistent with age. No acute intracranial process.

Brain MRI reveals a large area of restricted diffusion with matching T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, including the left insular ribbon and basal ganglia. There is associated mild local mass effect on the left lateral ventricle but no midline shift or hemorrhage.

Impression: Acute ischemic stroke in the left MCA territory. Magnetic resonance angiography is recommended to evaluate for large vessel occlusion or stenosis.

MRI of the brain demonstrates herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 7 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. There is crowding of the craniocervical junction, but the third and fourth ventricles are normal in size. Screening sagittal imaging of the cervical spine reveals no evidence of a syrinx.

Impression: Chiari I malformation with 7 mm tonsillar ectopia and craniocervical crowding. No associated syringomyelia or hydrocephalus. Findings are relevant for obstetric/anesthesia planning prior to scheduled delivery.

Cardiac MRI shows normal overall cardiac structure and function. The left ventricular end-diastolic volume index is 71 mL/m² and the right ventricular end-diastolic volume index is 68 mL/m². Left ventricular ejection fraction is 65% and right ventricular ejection fraction is 59%. There are no regional wall motion abnormalities or evidence of chamber enlargement.

No late gadolinium enhancement is identified. The pericardium is normal in thickness with no effusion, and the coronary arteries demonstrate normal origins. Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. No evidence of myocardial pathology, valvular dysfunction, or congenital cardiac defect.

Fetal MR imaging at 24 weeks gestation reveals classic signs of a Chiari II malformation. There is herniation of the cerebellar vermis into the upper cervical canal, accompanied by a small posterior fossa and a 'banana-shaped' cerebellum. Mild ventriculomegaly is present with the ventricular atrium measuring 12.1 mm. Severe splaying of the posterior elements of the lower lumbar spine is visualized starting at the L4 level through S1, with an overlying, fluid-filled sac measuring 2.4 cm, consistent with a myelomeningocele.

The fetal brain shows expected sulcation and gyration for 24 weeks gestation. Impression: Fetal Chiari II malformation and associated lumbosacral myelomeningocele. Pediatric neurosurgery and fetal therapy consultations are recommended.

Fetal MRI performed at 31 weeks gestation for evaluation of suspected thoracic anomaly. There is a large left-sided diaphragmatic defect with herniation of the stomach, several loops of small bowel, and a portion of the left hepatic lobe into the left hemithorax. This herniation causes a significant mediastinal shift to the right and marked compression of both the left and right lungs. The total fetal lung volume (TFLV) is measured at 18.4 mL, which is significantly reduced for gestational age, consistent with moderate-to-severe pulmonary hypoplasia. Intracranial structures demonstrate normal sulcation and ventricles within normal limits with the left atrium measuring 6.4 mm.

Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) with intrathoracic herniation of stomach, bowel, and liver. Associated mediastinal shift and severe bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia.

MR imaging of the brain and orbits reveals flattening of the posterior sclera bilaterally, with mild intraocular protrusion of the optic nerve heads. The optic nerve sheaths are prominent and distended with CSF. There is also moderate partial empty sella turcica, with no mass lesions, venous thrombosis, or hydrocephalus.

Impression: Intracranial and orbital signs consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). Clinical correlation with fundoscopy and lumbar puncture is recommended.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates completely normal structural fetal development. The cerebral cortex shows highly advanced and appropriate third-trimester sulcation and gyration, including well-defined secondary and tertiary sulci in both cerebral hemispheres. The lateral ventricular atria are symmetric and measure 6.2 mm. The cerebellum, vermis, and brainstem show normal morphology.

The fetal thoracic cavity, abdomen, kidneys, bladder, and spine are fully intact without any visible morphological abnormality. Normal amniotic fluid volume. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating appropriate fetal brain maturity and completely unremarkable anatomy.

Fetal MRI performed at 32 weeks gestation to evaluate fetal growth restriction. The single fetus is imaged in multiple projections. Intracranial structures demonstrate normal morphology. The lateral ventricular atrial measurements are symmetric at 6.0 mm bilaterally, which is well within normal limits. The sulcation and gyration pattern is normal for 32 weeks gestation, with well-formed cingulate, calcarine, and parieto-occipital sulci, as well as developing secondary sulci.

The fetal thoracic volume, abdomen, kidneys, and extremities are morphologically normal. Amniotic fluid volume is borderline low, but no specific fetal anomalies are seen. Impression: Normal fetal brain morphology and age-appropriate sulcation pattern. No structural anomalies detected.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate atypical chest discomfort in a 52-year-old male with borderline stress test results. The study shows normal left and right ventricular chamber dimensions and wall thicknesses. Systolic function is excellent, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63% and a right ventricular ejection fraction of 58%. No regional wall motion abnormalities are present.

First-pass myocardial perfusion during adenosine stress and rest imaging shows uniform contrast enhancement throughout the myocardium, with no inducible perfusion defects. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging is negative for scar. Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. No evidence of myocardial ischemia, infarction, or cardiomyopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reveals an acute cortical and subcortical area of restricted diffusion in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, demonstrating hyperintensity on DWI and corresponding hypointensity on ADC mapping. Associated subtle mass effect with effacement of neighboring sulci is present, without evidence of hemorrhagic transformation on susceptibility-weighted imaging.

Impression: Acute ischemic infarct of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory. No acute intracranial hemorrhage visualized.

Multiplanar brain MRI demonstrates normal cortical sulcation and ventricular size. There is no evidence of restricted diffusion on DWI sequences to suggest acute ischemia, and no signs of intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect. The venous sinuses demonstrate normal flow voids, and no abnormal meningeal enhancement is observed.

Impression: Unremarkable MR imaging of the brain. No structural, inflammatory, or vascular abnormalities are identified to explain the patient's persistent postpartum headache.

Brain MRI demonstrates hyperintense signal within the basal cisterns and the bilateral sylvian fissures on FLAIR sequences, indicating acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) confirms focal blooming in these areas. There is mild associated dilatation of the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles, suggesting early communicating hydrocephalus.

Impression: Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage localized predominantly within the basal cisterns and sylvian fissures. Mild early communicating hydrocephalus is noted; urgent vascular imaging (CTA or catheter angiography) is advised to rule out a ruptured aneurysm.

The study demonstrates normal cerebral ventricles, cisterns, and cortical sulci. There is no evidence of intracranial mass, mass effect, or midline shift. The brainstem, cerebellum, and visual pathways are unremarkable. Intracranial vascular structures are normal in course and caliber.

Impression: Normal MR examination of the brain. No intracranial pathology identified to account for symptoms of dizziness and transient vertigo.

Fetal MRI performed at 22 weeks gestation for evaluation of fetal intracranial structures. The brain demonstrates normal, age-appropriate structural development. The cerebral hemispheres exhibit a smooth parenchymal outline, with the primary fissure development matching the gestational milestone. The ventricular system is normal in size, with the atrial width measuring 6.0 mm bilaterally. The corpus callosum is visible and intact, and the posterior fossa structures including the cerebellum and brainstem appear completely normal.

Visualized fetal neck, spine, chest, abdomen, and limbs demonstrate normal morphology. Amniotic fluid volume is subjectively normal. Impression: Completely normal fetal MRI study for 22 weeks gestation, showing no structural or intracranial abnormalities.

Brain MRI performed for atypical aura and new-onset migraines. The cerebral parenchyma is structurally normal without focal lesions, areas of abnormal signal, or restriction of diffusion. There are no signs of intracranial hemorrhage or pathologic enhancement. The ventricles and extra-axial CSF spaces are unremarkable.

Impression: Completely normal brain MRI. No structural, demyelinating, or vascular abnormalities are present to explain the patient's migraine symptoms.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 24-year-old pregnant patient (20 weeks gestation) with a newly detected systolic murmur. There is a large defect in the mid-atrial septum measuring 2.4 cm, consistent with a secundum atrial septal defect (ASD). Phase-contrast flow imaging demonstrates a significant left-to-right shunt with a Qp/Qs ratio of 1.9. There is marked dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, indicating volume overload.

Right ventricular ejection fraction is preserved at 55%. The left ventricular size and function are normal (EF 60%). No pulmonary hypertension is suggested by ventricular septal contour. Impression: Large secundum atrial septal defect with significant left-to-right shunt and consequent right-sided cardiac chamber volume overload. Hemodynamics remain stable during pregnancy.

Cardiac MR imaging demonstrates normal cardiac chambers and valvular structure. All cardiac valves are morphologically normal with no significant stenosis or regurgitation. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 63%, and right ventricular ejection fraction is 58%. There is no evidence of focal myocardial hypertrophy, edema, or late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. No underlying structural, functional, or valvular disease is identified to account for the patient's functional murmur.

Brain MRI was performed for evaluation of severe postpartum headaches and visual disturbances. Multiplanar FLAIR and T2-weighted images demonstrate areas of bilateral, symmetric increased signal intensity within the subcortical white matter of the parieto-occipital lobes. No evidence of acute infarct, intracranial hemorrhage, or dural venous sinus thrombosis is seen. There is no mass effect or herniation.

Impression: Radiographic findings of vasogenic edema in the parieto-occipital regions, highly characteristic of Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) in this clinical context. Correlate with maternal blood pressures and clinical management of preeclampsia/eclampsia.

Fetal MRI at 33 weeks gestation demonstrates a large multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) on the left. The left kidney is enlarged and replaced by multiple non-communicating, thin-walled cysts of varying sizes, with no identifiable normal renal parenchyma. The contralateral right kidney appears completely normal in size, position, and signal intensity. Amniotic fluid volume is within normal limits. Intracranial sulcation and ventricular size (atrial width 6.0 mm) are normal.

The fetal bladder is well-filled, indicating preserved renal function from the functioning right kidney. Impression: Left multicystic dysplastic kidney. The right kidney is normal, and there is no evidence of oligohydramnios or secondary pulmonary hypoplasia.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 30-year-old female presenting with frequent ventricular extrasystoles and atypical chest pain. Cine sequences demonstrate bileaflet mitral valve prolapse (MVP), most pronounced in the posterior leaflet. There is clear evidence of mitral annular disjunction (MAD), measuring approximately 7.2 mm in the longitudinal axis during end-systole. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 58%.

Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging shows focal, patchy hyperenhancement localized to the mid-myocardium of the inferobasal wall and within the papillary muscles. Impression: Mitral valve prolapse with prominent mitral annular disjunction and localized papillary muscle and inferobasal myocardial fibrosis. This constellation represents an arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse phenotype.

Fetal MRI at 20 weeks gestation shows completely normal early cerebral development. Symmetrical lateral ventricles measure 5.2 mm at the atria. Smooth cortical surfaces are visualized, matching the expected normal pattern of sulcation and migration for 20 weeks. The spinal canal and cord are intact.

Visceral anatomy in the chest and abdomen appears unremarkable, and amniotic fluid volume is normal. Impression: Unremarkable fetal MRI demonstrating normal anatomy at 20 weeks gestation.

Brain MRI was evaluated with standard sequences. No intra- or extra-axial mass lesions, areas of acute ischemic infarction, or evidence of hemorrhage are identified. Ventricles and cortical sulci are unremarkable for patient age. Paranasal sinuses are clear.

Impression: Unremarkable and normal brain MRI. No intracranial pathology is present to explain chronic migraine headaches.

Cardiac MRI reveals normal maternal cardiac structures and functional parameters. Biventricular volumes and mass are within normal limits for a third-trimester pregnant patient. The left ventricular ejection fraction is 61%. No late gadolinium enhancement is present. Visualized fetal structures in the background are unremarkable.

Impression: Normal maternal cardiac MRI study. There is no evidence of structural cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, or chamber dilation to explain the patient's exertional dyspnea in late pregnancy.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation reveals severe skeletal dysplasia. There is marked, symmetric rhizomelic shortening of the bilateral femurs and humeri, measuring below the 5th percentile for gestational age. The fetal thorax is extremely narrow and bell-shaped, with shortened ribs. Fetal lung volumes are severely reduced (total lung volume 9.5 mL, representing severe pulmonary hypoplasia). Macrocephaly with frontal bossing is also noted.

Intracranial anatomy is structurally normal, and the ventricles are non-dilated with atrial width of 6.2 mm. Impression: Severe skeletal dysplasia with characteristics suggestive of thanatophoric dysplasia or achondroplasia. Significant narrow-thorax-induced pulmonary hypoplasia is present.

Cardiac MRI shows marked dilation and global dysfunction of the right ventricle, with an RVEF of 28% and significant regional wall motion abnormalities including right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) dyskinesis. Cine imaging and T1-weighted sequences demonstrate focal thinning and fatty infiltration of the right ventricular free wall. The left ventricle has a preserved ejection fraction of 58%.

Impression: Structural and functional abnormalities highly indicative of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting major Task Force criteria.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate for suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy in a patient presenting 3 weeks postpartum with progressive dyspnea and lower extremity edema. The left ventricle is moderately dilated with a left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (LVEDVI) of 110 mL/m2. There is global hypokinesis of the left ventricle with a severely reduced ejection fraction calculated at 32%. No definite regional wall motion abnormalities or intracardiac thrombi are identified. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging shows no evidence of myocardial infarction or focal replacement fibrosis.

Impression: Severe global left ventricular dysfunction and chamber dilatation, consistent with peripartum cardiomyopathy. No late gadolinium enhancement to suggest myocardial scarring or alternative etiology.

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks 2 days gestation demonstrates a large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The stomach, multiple loops of small and large bowel, and a portion of the left lobe of the liver are herniated into the left thoracic cavity. This has resulted in a severe mediastinal shift to the right, causing significant compression of the right lung. The observed total fetal lung volume is severely reduced, calculated at approximately 45% of the expected volume for this gestational age. The fetal brain shows normal age-appropriate development.

Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with herniation of stomach, bowel, and liver, associated with severe bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia and mediastinal shift. Recommend close multidisciplinary perinatal management.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates asymmetric septal hypertrophy, with the interventricular septum measuring 18 mm. Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction is present, exacerbated during systole with associated systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve, producing a moderate-to-severe posteriorly directed mitral regurgitant jet. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging reveals focal, patchy mid-myocardial enhancement at the anterior and posterior right ventricular insertion points.

Impression: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with significant LVOT obstruction and mitral regurgitation. Fibrosis noted at RV insertion points serves as a marker of risk for ventricular arrhythmia.

Brain MRI demonstrates two focal, round lesions within the left parietal cortex (1.2 cm) and right frontal lobe (0.8 cm) which exhibit high T1 signal intensity and surrounding vasogenic edema, consistent with hemorrhagic metastases. Follow-up imaging is correlated with a history of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

Impression: Multiple hemorrhagic brain lesions highly suspicious for metastatic disease, particularly gestational choriocarcinoma given the patient's medical history. Prompt clinical staging and oncology consultation are advised.

Cardiac MRI was completed using a comprehensive stress perfusion protocol with adenosine. No inducible perfusion defects are observed during peak hyperemia, and myocardial rest perfusion is normal. Left and right ventricular chamber sizes, wall thickness, and systolic functions are normal (LVEF 63%). No late gadolinium enhancement is detected.

Impression: Normal stress and rest perfusion cardiac MRI. No evidence of inducible myocardial ischemia, prior myocardial infarction, or structural heart disease.

Brain MR imaging demonstrates mild to moderate cerebral atrophy with prominence of the cerebral sulci and lateral ventricles, consistent with the patient's age. There are scattered bilateral subcortical and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, without associated mass effect, enhancement, or diffusion restriction.

Impression: Age-appropriate brain parenchymal changes and mild chronic microvascular ischemic disease. No acute infarction, hemorrhage, or mass lesion identified.

Brain MRI shows a prominent area of restricted diffusion in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, involving the left insula and adjacent temporal cortex, seen as hyperintensity on DWI and corresponding hypointensity on ADC maps. Minimal mass effect is observed on the left lateral ventricle, with no midline shift. No intracranial hemorrhage is identified.

Impression: Acute ischemic infarction within the left MCA territory. Recommend immediate clinical correlation and stroke management protocol.

Brain MRI shows low-lying cerebellar tonsils projecting approximately 7.5 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. There is crowding of the craniocervical junction. The cervical spinal cord was evaluated to the level of C4, revealing no evidence of a syrinx.

Impression: Chiari I malformation. No evidence of obstructive hydrocephalus or associated cervical syringomyelia on the visualized sequences.

Cardiac MRI reveals a bicuspid aortic valve with fusion of the left and right coronary cusps. The aortic valve demonstrates restricted opening, with a planimetered aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2, consistent with severe aortic stenosis. There is mild, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with an end-diastolic wall thickness of 13 mm. Global left ventricular systolic function is preserved with an ejection fraction of 54%.

Impression: Bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic stenosis and mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Dilated ascending aorta measuring 4.2 cm is also noted.

Fetal MRI performed at 25 weeks 1 day gestation. Evaluation of the fetal brain demonstrates normal gyral development and sulcation. The ventricular system is completely symmetric and non-dilated, with ventricular atria measuring 6.2 mm. The corpus callosum and posterior fossa elements are well-visualized and structurally normal.

The chest, abdomen, spine, and extremities are morphologically appropriate for gestational age. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study with no structural anomalies or developmental delays identified.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation reveals a large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). The stomach, left lobe of the liver, and multiple loops of small bowel have herniated into the left thoracic cavity, causing a severe mediastinal shift to the right. The observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/e LHR) is estimated at 38%, signifying moderate to severe pulmonary hypoplasia. The fetal brain is normal with an atrial width of 5.8 mm and age-appropriate sulcation.

Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic liver herniation and associated pulmonary hypoplasia. Prenatal counseling with pediatric surgery is indicated.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates highly mature, age-appropriate gyral and sulcal configuration. Secondary and tertiary sulcation are well-developed throughout the cerebral hemispheres. The lateral ventricles are completely normal in size and symmetric, with the atria measuring 6.4 mm. The corpus callosum is thick, well-visualized, and anatomically normal. Posterior fossa structures are entirely normal.

Thoracic and abdominal organs show normal anatomical structure and placement. Impression: Completely normal, unremarkable third-trimester fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation.

Dedicated pituitary MR protocol shows a well-circumscribed, hypointense mass on T1-weighted images within the left lateral aspect of the adenohypophysis, measuring 1.2 x 1.1 x 0.9 cm. The lesion demonstrates delayed contrast enhancement compared to the surrounding normal pituitary gland. There is mild superior expansion causing minimal displacement of the optic chiasm, with no invasion into the bilateral cavernous sinuses.

Impression: Pituitary macroadenoma. Clinical correlation with endocrine markers (prolactin levels) and formal visual field testing is recommended.

Cardiac MRI shows severe hypokinesis to akinesis of the apical and mid-ventricular segments of the left ventricle, with preserved contractility and hyperkinesis of the basal segments, resulting in classic apical ballooning. The overall left ventricular ejection fraction is acutely reduced to 38%. There is no evidence of obstructive coronary artery disease on recent angiographic records.

Late gadolinium enhancement imaging is negative for myocardial infarction or focal subendocardial scar, supporting a transient process. Impression: Left ventricular apical ballooning syndrome, highly consistent with Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy. No evidence of myocardial infarction.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, which measures up to 1.7 cm anteriorly and 1.2 cm adjacent to the right ventricular free wall. Mild diastolic compression of the right atrium is noted, although ventricular filling dynamics appear preserved. No sign of myocardial edema or delayed enhancement is noted within the myocardium itself.

Left ventricular and right ventricular cavity sizes and systolic functions are normal (LVEF 63%, RVEF 55%). The pericardium is mildly thickened and shows enhancement on late imaging. Impression: Moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with mild features of elevated intrapericardial pressure and active pericardial inflammation.

High-resolution sagittal and coronal T1-weighted images through the sella turcica, both before and after dynamic gadolinium administration, reveal a well-defined hypoenhancing lesion within the left lateral wing of the adenohypophysis measuring approximately 6 x 5 mm. There is subtle tilt of the pituitary stalk to the right, but the optic chiasm is structurally uninvolved with normal suprasellar cistern spacing. The remaining brain parenchyma is unremarkable.

Impression: Findings are highly consistent with a pituitary microadenoma of the left adenohypophysis. Clinical correlation with serum prolactin levels is suggested.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates urinary tract findings highly indicative of posterior urethral valves. The fetal bladder is severely distended with significant thickening and irregularity of the wall. The proximal urethra is dilated, creating a keyhole sign. There is severe bilateral hydronephrosis and dilated, tortuous ureters. Moderate oligohydramnios is present.

The brain shows complex, age-appropriate sulcation patterns with normal ventricular size (atrium measuring 6.5 mm). Impression: Posterior urethral valves with severe bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, bladder outlet obstruction, and moderate oligohydramnios.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 42-year-old female with a known systolic murmur. There is marked prolapse of the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve (P2 segment) into the left atrium during systole, associated with a severe eccentric jet of mitral regurgitation. The left atrium is significantly dilated (volume index of 48 mL/m²), and the left ventricle is mildly dilated with preserved systolic function (LVEF 64%).

Impression: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to posterior mitral valve leaflet prolapse (myxomatous mitral valve disease). Associated mild left ventricular and moderate left atrial dilation.

Cardiac MRI evaluates an adult female with repaired Tetralogy of Fallot. There is severe dilation of the right ventricle (RVEDVI of 165 mL/m2) with moderate right ventricular systolic dysfunction (RVEF of 36%). Marked, severe pulmonary regurgitation is quantified with a regurgitant fraction of 46%. Left ventricular volume and systolic function are preserved with an LVEF of 55%. No significant residual ventricular septal defect is identified.

Impression: Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot with severe pulmonary regurgitation, severe right ventricular dilation, and moderate RV systolic dysfunction. Findings strongly suggest the need for pulmonary valve replacement.

Cardiac MRI evaluates adult congenital heart disease status post childhood surgical correction for Tetralogy of Fallot. The right ventricle is severely dilated with a right ventricular end-diastolic volume index of 155 mL/m2. Quantitative flow analysis of the main pulmonary artery demonstrates severe pulmonary regurgitation with a regurgitant fraction of 42%. Right ventricular systolic function is mildly reduced with an ejection fraction of 45%.

Impression: Severe right ventricular volume overload and dilation second to severe pulmonary regurgitation, a common late sequela of repaired Tetralogy of Fallot. Findings provide quantitative support for potential pulmonary valve replacement.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate for peripartum cardiomyopathy in a 29-year-old female presenting with progressive dyspnea two weeks postpartum. The left ventricle is globally dilated with a diastolic diameter of 5.8 cm and demonstrates severe diffuse hypokinesis. The left ventricular ejection fraction is significantly reduced at 32%. No focal myocardial scar or late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is observed, suggesting the absence of prior ischemic infarction.

Impression: Findings are highly consistent with acute peripartum cardiomyopathy. No evidence of myocardial infarction or myocarditis. Urgent clinical management and medical therapy for heart failure are recommended, with close follow-up imaging.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates significant dilatation of the right ventricle, with a right ventricular end-diastolic volume index of 115 mL/m2. Regional dyskinesis and aneurysm formation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract are visualized. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging reveals patchy transmural enhancement within the right ventricular free wall.

Impression: Findings meet major Task Force criteria for Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC). Left ventricular size and systolic function (LVEF 55%) are preserved.

Fetal MRI performed at 22 weeks 4 days gestation demonstrates normal intracranial anatomy. The cerebral hemispheres exhibit appropriate primary sulcation, with well-demarcated sylvian fissures for this gestational age. The bilateral lateral ventricles are symmetric, with the atrial width measuring 5.5 mm. The corpus callosum is clearly visualized and intact. The posterior fossa, including the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, shows no abnormality.

Fetal chest, abdomen, spine, and extremities are grossly normal. There is normal amniotic fluid volume. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating age-appropriate structural brain development and no identifiable fetal anomalies.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation. Visualized brain morphology shows highly mature sulcation and operculization, matching expected third-trimester standards. The cerebral ventricular system is fully within normal limits, with a symmetric atrial measurement of 6.0 mm. No extra-axial hemorrhages, fluid collections, or chest anomalies are identified. Placenta and amniotic fluid volume are normal.

Impression: Normal fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation, demonstrating appropriate cortical maturation and normal intracranial anatomy.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). The stomach, small bowel loops, and a portion of the left hepatic lobe have herniated into the left thoracic cavity, causing a significant shift of the mediastinum to the right and severe compression of both lungs. Fetal lung-to-head ratio (LHR) and lung volumes are severely reduced. Intracranial structures show normal morphology. The lateral ventricular atrium measures 6.0 mm, and the cortical sulcation pattern is appropriate for 29 weeks.

The spine, kidneys, and extremities are morphologically intact. Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia containing stomach, bowel, and partial liver, leading to significant mediastinum shift and lung compression. Fetal brain development is normal.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks 2 days gestation reveals normal intracranial structures. The cerebral cortex shows expected opercularization of the sylvian fissure and secondary sulcation appropriate for late second trimester. The lateral ventricular system is normal in size, with symmetric atrial measurements of 6.0 mm. No extra-axial fluid collections or signs of cortical migration disorder are seen.

Fetal thoracic, abdominal viscera, and spinal column are intact. The placenta is posteriorly located and unremarkable. Impression: Completely unremarkable fetal MRI with appropriate development of cerebral sulcation and normal ventricular measurements.

Fetal MRI at 34 weeks gestation demonstrates a single intrauterine fetus in a cephalic presentation. Cortical sulcation and gyration are well-developed and completely appropriate for 34 weeks, demonstrating well-defined parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci. The lateral ventricles are symmetric, with atrial diameters measuring 6.2 mm. The corpus callosum and posterior fossa are structurally intact.

Fetal chest, lungs, and abdomen show normal signal intensity and morphology. No musculoskeletal anomalies are identified. Impression: Unremarkable fetal MRI demonstrating normal progress and age-appropriate fetal brain maturation.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation shows a right-sided diaphragmatic defect. The liver and a portion of the colon have herniated into the right thoracic cavity, causing leftward displacement of the mediastinum and compression of both lungs. The left lung is moderately compressed, and the calculated total fetal lung volume is reduced for 28 weeks gestation.

Impression: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver-up herniation, indicating a higher risk of pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks 5 days gestation demonstrates a large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). The stomach, several loops of small bowel, and a portion of the left hepatic lobe have herniated into the left hemithorax, causing a significant rightward mediastinal shift. The left lung is severely compressed and hypoplastic, with the observed-to-expected total fetal lung volume calculated at approximately 34%. Fetal brain imaging reveals normal sulcation and lateral ventricular atria measuring 6.1 mm.

Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic herniation of stomach, bowel, and partial liver, leading to significant mass effect, mediastinal shift, and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia.

T2-weighted and gradient-echo (GRE/SWI) imaging demonstrates a 'popcorn-like' lesion measuring 1.2 cm in the central pons, characterized by a reticulated core of mixed signal intensity and a complete hemosiderin rim. There is no surrounding edema or mass effect on the fourth ventricle.

Impression: Classic appearance of a brainstem (pontine) cavernous malformation (cavernoma) with evidence of chronic, clinically silent microhemorrhage. No acute bleeding or mass effect.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 54-year-old male with a history of anterior myocardial infarction. Cine images reveal localized dyskinesis and marked thinning of the mid-to-apical anterior wall and apex. The left ventricular chamber is mildly dilated, with a measured left ventricular ejection fraction of 38%. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) sequences demonstrate intense, transmural enhancement (>75% thickness) involving the apical anterior and anteroseptal segments, consistent with a completed, non-viable infarct territory.

Impression: Chronic, transmural anterior and anteroseptal myocardial infarction in the LAD distribution. The affected segments demonstrate non-viability based on transmural late gadolinium enhancement.

Brain MRI performed for evaluation of refractory gestational migraines. The brain parenchyma shows normal signal intensity throughout without focal ischemic lesions, masses, or areas of abnormal signal. The ventricular system, sulci, and cisterns are within normal limits for the patient's age. The major vascular flow voids are intact.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain with no structural or vascular abnormalities. No etiology identified for the patient's clinical presentation of migraines.

Cardiac MRI obtained for evaluation of atypical chest pain and palpitations. Quantitative analysis demonstrates normal left ventricular cavity size and wall thickness, with a left ventricular end-diastolic volume of 112 mL and normal left ventricular mass index. Segmental and global left ventricular systolic function is excellent with a calculated ejection fraction of 64%. The right ventricle is normal in size and function with an RVEF of 59%. There is no evidence of myocardial edema, perfusion abnormalities, or late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Unremarkable cardiac MRI. Normal chamber dimensions and biventricular systolic function, with no evidence of myocardial ischemia or fibrosis.

MR imaging of the brain demonstrates a large, heterogeneous, ring-enhancing mass centered within the right temporal lobe, measuring 4.8 x 4.2 x 3.9 cm. The mass is surrounded by extensive vasogenic edema eliciting significant mass effect, with partial compression of the right lateral ventricle and a 6 mm leftward midline shift. Foci of central necrosis and internal microhemorrhage are noted.

Impression: Aggressive, large, ring-enhancing right temporal lobe mass with significant mass effect and midline shift, highly suspicious for high-grade glioma (such as glioblastoma). Neurosurgical intervention is urgently indicated.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates fully matured cerebral architecture. Cortical folding is highly advanced and appropriate for 35 weeks, with clear development of secondary and tertiary sulci. The lateral ventricles are completely normal, with the atrium measuring 5.5 mm on both sides. The corpus callosum, optic chiasm, and brainstem are completely normal in appearance.

No focal abnormalities are seen in the chest, abdomen, or spine. Placentation is posterior and uncomplicated. Impression: Entirely normal third-trimester fetal MRI study demonstrating reassuring neurological and structural development.

Cardiac MRI performed for atypical chest pain demonstrates normal left and right ventricular volumes and systolic function. LVEF is 62%, and RVEF is 57%. No myocardial edema is seen on T2-weighted imaging, and there is absolutely no evidence of late gadolinium enhancement to suggest myocardial scarring or fibrosis. Valvular structures are normal.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI with preserved biventricular function and no evidence of structural heart disease, ischemia, or inflammation.

Brain MRI demonstrates bilateral, relatively symmetric areas of high T2 and FLAIR signal intensity localized to the subcortical white matter and cortex of the parieto-occipital lobes. Minimal mass effect is associated, without restricted diffusion on DWI sequences or abnormal contrast enhancement. The findings are characteristic of vasogenic edema.

Impression: Vasogenic edema in a classic parieto-occipital distribution, highly consistent with Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES), clinically correlating with severe preeclampsia/eclampsia. Recommend clinical monitoring and blood pressure management.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation reveals severe, absolute oligohydramnios. Both renal fossae are empty, and no renal tissue or renal arteries are identifiable, consistent with bilateral renal agenesis. The urinary bladder is non-visualized. There is mild crowding of the fetal parts and compression of the thorax. The fetal brain is structurally intact with an atrial width of 6.2 mm; early sulcation is present.

Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis with anhydramnios, representing classic Potter's sequence features. Extremely guarded prognosis.

Multiplanar brain MRI was performed using high-resolution anatomical sequences. There is no evidence of intracranial mass, abnormal extra-axial fluid collections, or focal signal abnormality within the brain parenchyma. The grey-white matter junction is preserved, and the ventricles are symmetric and unremarkable. The mastoid air cells and paranasal sinuses are fully aerated.

Impression: Normal magnetic resonance imaging of the brain. No structural, inflammatory, or ischemic explanation for the patient's headache workup.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation reveals a large multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) on the right side, characterized by multiple non-communicating cysts of varying sizes and minimal residual renal parenchyma. The contralateral left kidney is normal in size and appearance, and amniotic fluid volume is completely normal. The fetal brain shows normal, age-appropriate sulcation patterns with lateral ventricular atria measuring 6.0 mm.

No other fetal anomalies are identified. Impression: Isolated unilateral right multicystic dysplastic kidney with a normal, functioning left kidney and normal amniotic fluid volume.

Cardiac MRI shows diffuse, concentric thickening of the left ventricular myocardium, with a maximal septal wall thickness of 18 mm. The right ventricular free wall is also mildly thickened. Bilateral atria are severely dilated. The left ventricular ejection fraction is reduced at 43%, demonstrating restrictive filling pathology on diastolic flow evaluation.

Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging shows diffuse, subendocardial hyperenhancement of non-coronary distribution, involving both ventricles and the atria. Native T1 values are severely elevated at 1240 ms. Impression: Highly classic findings of cardiac amyloidosis with characteristic diffuse subendocardial LGE and restrictive physiology.

Brain MRI demonstrates ventricular enlargement that is disproportionate to the degree of cerebral sulcal atrophy. Prominent dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles is seen, with rounding of the frontal horns and thinning/elevation of the corpus callosum. A hyperdynamic CSF flow void is observed within the aqueduct of Sylvius on T2-weighted imaging. No focal masses or acute ischemic lesions are present.

Impression: Ventriculomegaly disproportionate to cortical atrophy, highly suggestive of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) in the appropriate clinical setting. Suggest clinical correlation with gait assessment and high-volume lumbar puncture.

Fetal MRI at 30 weeks gestation demonstrates diffuse, symmetric shortening of all long bones, consistent with severe rhizomelic micromelia. The thorax is narrow and bell-shaped, but no fractures of the ribs or long bones are detected. The skull shows prominent frontal bossing, but normal mineralization.
