These lesions do not demonstrate restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC mapping, indicating vasogenic rather than cytotoxic edema. Ventricles and basal cisterns are within normal limits.

Impression: Bilateral parietal and occipital vasogenic edema patterns, classic for Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES). In this obstetric patient, this is highly indicative of severe preeclampsia/eclampsia complications.

Brain MRI demonstrating symmetric, patchy areas of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity within the cortical and subcortical white matter of the bilateral parieto-occipital lobes. There is no evidence of restricted diffusion on DWI sequences or significant mass effect. The patient is currently postpartum with a history of severe preeclampsia.

Impression: Findings are highly characteristic of Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) in the setting of postpartum preeclampsia. Clinical monitoring and blood pressure control are recommended.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks 6 days gestation. The right kidney is normal in size and signal intensity. The left kidney is markedly enlarged and replaced by multiple, non-communicating cysts of varying sizes, with the largest measuring 2.1 cm. There is no identifiable normal renal parenchyma on the left. Amniotic fluid volume is normal, suggesting adequate renal function from the contralateral right kidney. The bladder is normally distended.

The fetal brain shows normal sulcation and ventricular size (atrial measurements of 6.2 mm). Impression: Left multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) with a normal contralateral right kidney and normal amniotic fluid volume.

Cardiac MRI reveals marked biatrial enlargement and significant prolapse of the posterior mitral valve leaflet (P2 segment) into the left atrium during systole. This results in an eccentric, anteriorly directed jet of severe mitral regurgitation. The left ventricular end-diastolic volume index is moderately increased at 112 mL/m2, representing chronic volume overload. LVEF is preserved at 56%.

Impression: Posterior mitral valve prolapse with severe mitral regurgitation and mild left ventricular remodeling. Recommend clinical correlation for surgical repair planning.

Brain MRI demonstrates mild, age-appropriate global cerebral atrophy and a few scattered, nonspecific foci of high T2/FLAIR signal in the deep white matter, likely reflecting mild chronic microvascular ischemic changes. There is no acute territorial infarct, hemorrhage, mass effect, or abnormal enhancement.

Impression: Mild, age-appropriate cerebral involutional changes and chronic microvascular white matter changes. No acute intracranial pathology.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates entirely normal intracranial anatomy. The cerebral cortex shows normal central, precentral, and postcentral sulci development, entirely appropriate for 29 weeks. The lateral ventricles are completely symmetric, with the left and right atrial widths measuring 6.3 mm.

The midline structure is normal with a well-developed corpus callosum. Fetal trunk and skeleton are intact. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating age-appropriate brain biometry and cortical development without anomalies.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was acquired using high-resolution structural and fluid-attenuated sequences. The brain parenchyma is normal in appearance without evidence of acute ischemia, hemorrhage, demyelinating plaques, or focal mass lesions. The ventricles, sulci, and cisterns are within normal limits for the patient's age. The major intracranial arterial flow voids are preserved.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain with no structural pathology identified to explain the patient's history of chronic migraine with aura.

MR evaluation demonstrates multiple small, hyperintense focal lesions on T2/FLAIR with surrounding edema within the grey-white matter junctions of both cerebral hemispheres. Several of these lesions exhibit blooming artifacts on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) indicating microhemorrhages, and show ring enhancement post-contrast.

Impression: Multiple hemorrhagic intra-axial lesions, highly suspicious for metastatic disease. In this young postpartum female, gestational trophoblastic disease (choriocarcinoma metastasis) is a prime consideration; clinical correlation with serum beta-hCG is urgently recommended.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation demonstrates partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior portion (genu and part of the body) of the corpus callosum is visualized, but the posterior body and splenium are absent. There is associated mild colpocephaly with prominence of the posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle, measuring 10.3 mm. The right lateral ventricular atrium is 8.5 mm. Sulcal development is appropriate for 31 weeks, with well-delineated central and cingulate sulci.

The cerebellum and posterior fossa structures are normal. No facial clefts or other midline anomalies are seen. Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with mild ventriculomegaly. Developmental pediatric follow-up is recommended.

Brain MRI shows extensive susceptibility artifact within the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and cerebral sulci, consistent with acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. There is mild associated ventriculomegaly involving the lateral and third ventricles, indicating early communicating hydrocephalus. MR angiography demonstrates a 6 mm saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery.

Impression: Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage secondary to a ruptured 6 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Early communicating hydrocephalus is also noted.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates multiple, patchy areas of mid-myocardial and subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in a non-coronary distribution, involving the basal anteroseptal and mid-lateral walls. Localized regional wall motion abnormalities are present in the corresponding lateral wall segments, and the left ventricular ejection fraction is mildly reduced at 46%.

T2-weighted and T2-mapping imaging demonstrate elevated signal intensity in the same regions, indicating active inflammatory edema. Impression: Cardiac MRI findings consistent with active myocardial sarcoidosis, exhibiting patchy non-ischemic LGE and associated localized active inflammation.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior portion (genu and anterior body) is present, but the posterior body and splenium are absent. There is associated mild colpocephaly with prominent occipital horns, and the left lateral ventricular atrium measures 10.2 mm while the right measures 9.9 mm. Cortical sulcation is normal and appropriate for 29 weeks.

The posterior fossa and remainder of the fetal brain are intact. Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with mild colpocephaly and normal cerebral sulcation.

Brain MR imaging demonstrates an enhancing, ice-cream-cone shaped mass centered within the left internal auditory canal with extension into the left cerebellopontine angle cistern. The lesion measures 1.8 x 1.4 cm and causes mild remodeling of the internal auditory canal and slight compression of the adjacent middle cerebellar peduncle. No hydrocephalus is present.

Impression: Enhancing mass in the left internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle, consistent with a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). Otolaryngology consult recommended.

Cardiac MRI with 3D angiographic reconstruction evaluates a young adult female with refractory hypertension. There is a discrete, focal narrowing of the proximal descending thoracic aorta, localized immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. The minimum luminal diameter at the coarctation site is 7 mm. Multiplanar imaging demonstrates prominent collateral internal mammary and intercostal arteries. The left ventricle demonstrates mild concentric hypertrophy, with an ejection fraction of 58%.

Impression: Classic post-ductal aortic coarctation with significant luminal narrowing and extensive collateral vessel formation. Associated mild left ventricular concentric hypertrophy.

Post-gadolinium brain MRI reveals nodular, leptomeningeal enhancement involving the cerebellar folia, basal cisterns, and hypothalamic region. Several small, non-enhancing parenchymal lesions are visible in the subcortical white matter. The ventricular system is normal in size. Optic chiasm shows mild thickening and enhancement.

Impression: Nodular leptomeningeal enhancement and hypothalamic involvement, which, in a patient with systemic sarcoidosis, is highly indicative of neurosarcoidosis. Recommend close follow-up.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 22 weeks gestation reveals completely normal intracranial structures. The cerebral hemispheres show appropriate and smooth early sulcation patterns expected for this gestational age. The lateral ventricles are symmetric, with the atrial diameter measuring 5.8 mm, well within the normal limit. The corpus callosum and brainstem appear fully formed and structurally intact.

Fetal cardiothoracic and abdominal organ anatomy are normal, with no evidence of diaphragmatic hernia, renal anomalies, or bowel dilatation. The spine shows normal segmentation and alignment. Impression: Unremarkable fetal MRI demonstrating normal anatomy and age-appropriate brain development.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 24 weeks gestation demonstrates normal anatomy. The cerebral hemispheres exhibit appropriate primary sulcation, including early perisylvian and parieto-occipital fissures consistent with 24 weeks gestation. The lateral ventricles are symmetric, with the atrial diameter measuring 6.2 mm. The corpus callosum, optic chiasm, brainstem, and cerebellum are unremarkable.

No chest masses, abdominal wall defects, or spinal anomalies are noted. Amniotic fluid volume is within normal parameters. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating appropriate intracranial structures and age-matched cortical folding.

Cardiac MRI of a 55-year-old male with a history of recurrent ventricular tachycardia. The right ventricle is severely dilated (RVEDVI 125 mL/m2) and demonstrates regional wall motion abnormalities, specifically aneurysmal outpouchings and dyskinesia of the RV free wall. The right ventricular ejection fraction is severely reduced at 32%. Left ventricular size, wall thickness, and systolic function are within normal limits (EF 58%). Late gadolinium enhancement is seen lining the right ventricular free wall.

Impression: Features are strongly indicative of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting multiple major Task Force criteria.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal left and right ventricular chamber dimensions and systolic function (LVEF 59%, RVEF 55%). However, there is a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, measuring up to 18 mm adjacent to the right atrium and 15 mm adjacent to the left ventricular apex. The pericardium appears thickened up to 4 mm and shows intense, late enhancement following gadolinium administration, indicative of active inflammation. No signs of diastolic chamber collapse (tamponade physiology) are visualized.

Impression: Moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with active pericarditis, demonstrated by diffuse pericardial thickening and enhancement. No current signs of cardiac tamponade.

Fetal MRI at 23 weeks gestation demonstrates bilateral, severely enlarged multicystic dysplastic kidneys (MCDK). Both renal fossae are occupied by giant, lobulated masses filled with non-communicating cysts of varying sizes, with virtually no normal parenchymal signal remaining. Marked oligohydramnios is present, causing extreme compression of the fetal trunk.

Intracranial anatomy is intact with a lateral ventricle atrial width of 6.3 mm and appropriate early sulcation. Impression: Bilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney disease with associated severe oligohydramnios. This carries a high risk of pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter's sequence) and requires urgent multidisciplinary counseling.

Cardiac MRI reveals a chronic subendocardial myocardial infarction involving the basal-to-mid inferior and inferoseptal walls (RCA territory), with late gadolinium enhancement spanning approximately 40% of the wall thickness. Akinesis of the inferior segments is observed. Left ventricular systolic function is moderately reduced with an estimated LVEF of 42%.

Impression: Chronic ischemic heart disease with subendocardial scar in the RCA vascular territory. Left ventricular remodeling and moderate systolic dysfunction.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation reveals partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior corpus callosum (genu and anterior body) is visualized, but the posterior body and splenium are absent. There is associated mild colpocephaly with prominent occipital horns of the lateral ventricles, measuring 11.2 mm on the left and 10.9 mm on the right. Sulcal development is normal.

No other structural abnormalities of the brainstem, cerebellum, or spine are identified. Fetal viscera are normal. Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated mild bilateral ventriculomegaly/colpocephaly. Recommend postnatal clinical and neurodevelopmental evaluation.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 68-year-old female with progressive exertional dyspnea and syncope. There is severe, asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximum diastolic wall thickness of 23 mm in the anterior basal septum. Dynamic cine sequences demonstrate systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve leaflet, resulting in severe left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and moderate mitral regurgitation. The left ventricular cavity is small, and systolic function is hyperdynamic with an ejection fraction of 72%.

Impression: Severe hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with prominent SAM and associated LVOT obstruction. Dense mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement is noted in the hypertrophied septum, reflecting myocardial fibrosis.

MRI brain study shows normal parenchymal signal and volume. No focal areas of restricted diffusion are observed on DWI/ADC, ruling out acute ischemic stroke. No abnormal intra- or extra-axial fluid accumulations, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or subdural hematoma are visible. The venous sinuses are patent and flow voids are normal.

Impression: Completely unremarkable brain MRI. No acute intracranial findings or trauma-related parenchymal injury detected.

Cardiac MRI was performed for follow-up evaluation of clinically diagnosed myocarditis from 12 months ago. T2 mapping shows normalization of myocardial relaxation times, suggesting complete resolution of previous myocardial edema. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging shows only a tiny, residual subepicardial focal area of fibrosis in the basal lateral wall, which has significantly decreased in size compared to the prior examination. Ventricular volumes are normal, and the ejection fraction is 61%.

Impression: Marked improvement of myocarditis with resolution of active edema and only a minimal residual subepicardial scar in the lateral wall. Global systolic function is completely normal.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation reveals normal fetal brain anatomy. The lateral ventricles measure 6.1 mm at the level of the atrium. Cortical sulcation is appropriate for 26 weeks, showing normal development of the parieto-occipital and cingulate sulci and well-defined sylvian fissures. The corpus callosum is intact and fully visualized.

No thoracic, abdominal, or skeletal abnormalities are identified. Amniotic fluid volume is normal. Impression: Normal fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation, indicating appropriate structural brain maturation and no detectable fetal anomalies.

Brain MRI demonstrates diffuse, nodular, and linear leptomeningeal enhancement along the cerebellar folia, brainstem, and basal cisterns. There are also several small parenchymal nodules in the cerebral cortex that demonstrate nodular contrast enhancement. Lumbar puncture correlates with elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis.

Impression: Leptomeningeal and parenchymal nodular enhancement, highly suspicious for neurosarcoidosis. Recommend correlation with systemic inflammatory markers and chest imaging.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 58-year-old female undergoing evaluation for suspected pulmonary hypertension. The study shows normal left ventricular size and function (LVEF 62%). Right ventricular volumes, wall thickness, and systolic function (RVEF 52%) are within normal physiological ranges. There is no evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy or flattening of the interventricular septum during diastole.

No late gadolinium enhancement of either ventricle is present. Impression: Normal cardiac MRI with no structural or functional evidence of right-sided chamber overload or pulmonary hypertensive heart disease (cor pulmonale) at this time.

MR imaging of the brain reveals bilateral, relatively symmetric areas of high T2 and FLAIR signal intensity involving the subcortical white matter of the parieto-occipital lobes. No restricted diffusion is demonstrated on DWI/ADC sequences, indicating vasogenic rather than cytotoxic edema. No mass effect or midline shift is identified.

Impression: Vasogenic edema in a classic parieto-occipital distribution, highly consistent with Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) in this postpartum patient. Clinical correlation with blood pressure and preeclampsia history is recommended.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation evaluates a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. There is a large left-sided diaphragmatic defect with herniation of the stomach, multiple small bowel loops, and a portion of the left hepatic lobe into the left hemithorax. This causes a significant mediastinal shift to the right side and severe compression of both lungs. The estimated fetal lung volume is severely reduced, calculated at approximately 35% of predicted value.

Intracranial anatomy is intact with normal ventricular atrial width (5.5 mm) and age-appropriate sulcation. Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) with severe pulmonary hypoplasia. High-risk perinatal management planning is indicated.

Brain MRI obtained with multiplanar and multisequence protocols. The cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem demonstrate normal signal intensity and morphology. There is no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, restriction of diffusion, mass effect, or anomalous extra-axial collections.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. Normal intracranial structures with no underlying pathology detected for presenting symptoms of intermittent dizziness.

Cardiac MRI was performed in a 31-year-old pregnant female (gestational age 20 weeks) presenting with a newly detected systolic murmur. Right and left ventricular dimensions, wall thickness, and volumes are well within normal physiologic limits. Calculated LVEF is 62% and RVEF is 58% without regional wall motion abnormalities. Valvular structures demonstrate normal anatomy and flow dynamics.

Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI showing no structural or functional abnormalities. Normal ventricular function, which is reassuring in the context of the patient's ongoing pregnancy.

Brain MRI demonstrates inferior herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum by approximately 7.5 mm. There is crowding of the craniocervical junction with effacement of the surrounding CSF spaces. High-resolution sagittal cervical spine sequences do not reveal any evidence of syrinx formation.

Impression: Chiari I malformation with 7.5 mm of tonsillar ectopia, resulting in mild crowding of the foramen magnum. No cervical syrinx or associated hydrocephalus is noted.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 19-year-old male with a history of Tetralogy of Fallot repaired in infancy. There is severe, free pulmonary regurgitation with a calculated regurgitant fraction of 48%. The right ventricle is severely dilated (RVEDV 165 mL/m²) with mild global hypokinesis and an RVEF of 41%. The left ventricle is normal in size and has normal systolic function (LVEF 58%).

Impression: Severe pulmonary regurgitation with subsequent severe right ventricular dilatation and mild RV dysfunction. This pattern is characteristic of late complications following repair of Tetralogy of Fallot.

Brain MRI demonstrates multiple discrete, ovoid, hyperintense T2/FLAIR lesions involving the periventricular white matter, corpus callosum, and subcortical white matter. Several of these lesions are oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles, consistent with Dawson's fingers. Following contrast administration, two active periventricular lesions demonstrate nodular enhancement.

Impression: Multiple demyelinating lesions showing dissemination in space and time, highly characteristic of active multiple sclerosis. Clinical correlation with CSF oligoclonal bands is recommended.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation demonstrates normal fetal development. Primary cortical sulcation is completely appropriate for gestational age, including symmetric Sylvian and parieto-occipital fissures. The cerebral ventricular system is normal in size, with atrial measurements of 6.1 mm. The midline structures, including the corpus callosum, are normal.

The fetal chest, abdomen, spine, and extremities show no structural defects. Amniotic fluid volume is unremarkable. Impression: Completely normal 24-week fetal MRI, with normal intracranial anatomy and no evidence of congenital malformations.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks 1 day gestation shows mature cortical development. Complex tertiary sulcation is demonstrated throughout both hemispheres, entirely appropriate for late third-trimester gestation. The ventricular system is normal in size and morphology; bilateral atrial measurements are 6.5 mm. Intracranial fluid-attenuated sequences show no signs of hemorrhage or infarction.

The thoracic, abdominal organs, and fetal spine are normal. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating mature cerebral sulcation and normal ventricles.

Brain MRI demonstrates diffuse, confluent T2/FLAIR hyperintensities within the bilateral periventricular and deep subcortical white matter. These changes sparing the subcortical U-fibers and brainstem are characteristic of chronic microvascular ischemic changes. Additionally, there are multiple punctate chronic microhemorrhages in the basal ganglia bilaterally, as visualized on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI).

Impression: Moderate to severe chronic microvascular ischemic white matter changes, along with chronic cerebral microhemorrhages, likely related to long-standing chronic hypertension or cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks 5 days gestation demonstrates normal fetal anatomy. The cerebral cortex shows appropriate sulcation and migration patterns for 25 weeks gestation, with well-formed Sylvian fissures and parieto-occipital sulci. The lateral ventricles are completely normal in caliber, with atria measuring 6.0 mm on the left and 5.8 mm on the right. The corpus callosum and cavum septum pellucidum are present and normal in appearance.

Fetal posterior fossa structures, including the cerebellum and brainstem, are within normal limits. The spine, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and extremities are normal. Impression: Normal, unremarkable fetal MRI study showing age-appropriate brain development.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates advanced, normal fetal brain development. The lateral ventricles are completely within normal limits, with the atrium measuring 6.5 mm bilaterally. The cortical gyration is highly complex and appropriate for 35 weeks, displaying well-developed primary, secondary, and early tertiary sulci. The corpus callosum and brainstem are structurally intact.

No visceral abnormalities of the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum are demonstrated. Spine and skeletal structures are fully intact. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating appropriate cerebral growth, advanced sulcation, and normal posterior fossa structures at 35 weeks gestation.

Brain MR imaging demonstrates mild generalized cortical atrophy and ventricular prominence, appropriate for the patient's age. There are several small, scattered foci of non-specific T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter, typical of chronic microvascular ischemic changes. No acute infarcts, hemorrhages, or mass lesions are present.

Impression: Age-appropriate brain MRI. Mild chronic microvascular ischemic changes are noted, but there is no acute intracranial abnormality or mass effect.

Cardiac MRI was completed using standardized steady-state free precession (SSFP) and delayed enhancement sequences. The left and right ventricular chambers are of normal dimensions, with normal ventricular myocardial thickness. Global and regional wall motion analysis is entirely normal. There is no evidence of delayed contrast enhancement or pericardial abnormal thickening.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. Normal biventricular volumes and preserved systolic function (LVEF 63%, RVEF 59%) with no evidence of myocarditis or fibrosis.

MRI brain without contrast was performed to evaluate chronic non-specific headache. The cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem are structurally normal. There are no signal abnormalities within the brain parenchyma, and the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces are appropriate in size and configuration for age. Visualized vascular structures show normal flow voids.

Impression: Normal MRI of the brain. No intracranial mass, acute ischemia, hemorrhage, or hydrocephalus is identified.

Brain MRI performed for transient paresthesias in a 33-year-old female shows no evidence of demyelinating disease, focal lesions, or acute ischemia. Brain parenchyma shows normal signal characteristics. Ventricles and extra-axial CSF spaces are within normal limits. The optic nerves and chiasm are normal.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. No structural, inflammatory, or demyelinating pathology detected.

MR imaging demonstrates a well-circumscribed, round, non-enhancing lesion measuring 1.2 x 1.1 cm located at the anterosuperior aspect of the third ventricle, adjacent to the foramen of Monro. The lesion is hyperintense on T1 and hypointense on T2 sequences, showing mild mass effect but no ventriculomegaly.

Impression: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle at the foramen of Monro. Although no hydrocephalus is present, periodic imaging surveillance is recommended to monitor for obstruction.

MR of the brain was obtained following a traumatic fall. No evidence of acute intracranial hemorrhage, extra-axial fluid collections, or parenchymal signal abnormality is identified. Susceptibility-weighted imaging shows no signs of diffuse axonal injury (DAI).

Impression: Normal MR of the brain with no structural or hemorrhagic correlates for post-concussive syndrome.

Brain MRI shows an irregular, thick-walled ring-enhancing intra-axial lesion centered within the right temporal lobe, measuring 4.5 x 3.8 cm. Significant central necrosis is observed within the mass, surrounded by extensive T2/FLAIR hyperintensity denoting severe vasogenic edema. Mass effect is evident, with compression of the right lateral ventricle and 6 mm of leftward midline shift.

Impression: High-grade primary intracranial neoplasm, highly suggestive of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). Recommend urgent neurosurgical evaluation.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates a large secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) measuring approximately 2.1 cm in the maximal diameter, resulting in significant left-to-right shunting. This has led to moderate dilatation of the right atrium and the right ventricle (right ventricular end-diastolic volume index of 135 mL/m2). The right ventricular ejection fraction is preserved at 52%. The left ventricle is normal in size with a preserved ejection fraction of 60%. Velocity-encoded phase-contrast imaging of the aorta and pulmonary artery reveals a significant pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp/Qs) estimated at 1.9.

Impression: Large secundum atrial septal defect with significant left-to-right shunt and consequent right-sided chamber dilatation. No evidence of pulmonary arterial hypertension is visualized on current imaging.

MRI demonstrates an infiltrative, non-enhancing, T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesion centered in the left frontal lobe subcortical white matter, measuring 3.1 x 2.8 x 2.5 cm. There is mild mass effect on the left lateral ventricle anterior horn, but no midline shift or herniation. DWI does not demonstrate restricted diffusion, and there is no surrounding vasogenic edema.

Impression: Infiltrative, non-enhancing left frontal lobe white matter lesion, highly consistent with a low-grade astrocytoma. Correlation with biopsy is recommended.

Multiplanar, multisequence brain MRI was performed to evaluate postpartum headaches. There is no evidence of intracranial mass, acute ischemia, or hemorrhage. The ventricles and sulci are normal in size and configuration, showing no signs of hydrocephalus. Visualized cerebral venous sinuses demonstrate normal flow voids without thrombosis.

Impression: Unremarkable brain MRI. No acute intracranial pathology or structural abnormality is identified to explain the postpartum headaches.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation demonstrates a large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). There is significant herniation of the stomach, multiple small bowel loops, and a portion of the left hepatic lobe into the left hemithorax. This herniation causes a severe rightward mediastinal shift and marked compression of both lungs, with the lung-to-head ratio (LHR) calculated to assess pulmonary hypoplasia. The fetal brain shows normal, age-appropriate sulcation patterns, and the lateral ventricles are normal with an atrial measurement of 5.9 mm.

No other congenital anomalies are observed in the spine or abdomen. Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver herniated into the chest and significant mediastinal shift. Findings raise concern for severe secondary pulmonary hypoplasia, warranting high-risk obstetrical and pediatric surgical management.

Cardiac MRI performed for the evaluation of persistent palpitations and frequent premature ventricular contractions. The left ventricular chamber dimensions and systolic function are normal (EF 61%). The right ventricular size, morphology, and wall motion are also entirely normal (EF 56%). There is no evidence of fatty infiltration of the right ventricular free wall, myocardial edema, or late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Unremarkable cardiac MRI. No structural abnormality, chamber enlargement, or myocardial scar is present to explain the palpitations.

Brain MRI including dedicated thin-slice sequences through the internal auditory canals (IACs) was performed. There is no evidence of vestibulocochlear nerve enhancement, cerebellopontine angle mass, or abnormal fluid collection. The brainstem, cerebellum, and cerebral hemispheres are structurally normal with no ischemic or inflammatory changes.

Impression: Unremarkable brain and IAC MRI. No structural abnormality, vestibulocochlear pathology, or central demyelinating disease is detected to account for vertigo.

MRI of the brain and posterior fossa demonstrates cerebellar tonsils herniating approximately 7 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. The tonsils are pointed in morphology. There is mild crowding of the craniocervical junction, but no evidence of syringomyelia within the visualized upper cervical spinal cord. The supratentorial brain parenchyma and ventricular system are normal.

Impression: Chiari I malformation, characterized by 7 mm cerebellar tonsillar herniation below the foramen magnum without associated syringomyelia on the visualized cervical spine. Clinical correlation with headache symptoms is recommended.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal left ventricular end-diastolic volume (122 mL) and preserved global systolic function with a calculated ejection fraction of 62%. The right ventricle is normal in size and function with an ejection fraction of 58%. No regional wall motion abnormalities are identified. Myocardial tissue characterization reveals normal T1 and T2 relaxation times with no focal areas of signal abnormality.

There is no evidence of late gadolinium enhancement to suggest myocardial scar, fibrosis, or active inflammation. Valvular flow patterns and velocities are within normal physiological limits. Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study showing preserved biventricular function and structure without signs of peripartum cardiomyopathy or myocardial injury.

Sagittal T1-weighted imaging reveals peg-like herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 8.5 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. There is crowding of the craniocervical junction. A thin, longitudinal fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) is visualized within the upper cervical spinal cord, extending from C2 to C4, measuring up to 3 mm in caliber.

Impression: Arnold-Chiari malformation Type I with an associated small, non-tension cervical syrinx.

MR imaging of the brain demonstrates diffuse hyperintense signal within the basal cisterns and right sylvian fissure on FLAIR sequences. Corresponding signal loss on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) confirms acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. There is mild enlargement of the lateral ventricles, suggesting early communicating hydrocephalus.

Impression: Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage centered in the basal cisterns and right sylvian fissure. Emergency CTA/MRA is recommended to evaluate for a ruptured intracranial aneurysm.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates normal anatomy. The brain hemispheres are symmetric with normal ventricular size; the atrium measures 5.9 mm. Early sulcal patterns, including the cingulate and calcarine sulci, are normal. Operculization of the temporal lobes is proceeding normally for 28 weeks.

All thoracic, abdominal, and skeletal structures are normal. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study at 28 weeks gestation, showing expected intracranial development.

Fetal MRI at 23 weeks gestation shows complete bilateral absence of renal tissue in the renal fossae or pelvic regions, confirming bilateral renal agenesis. There is profound oligohydramnios (anhydramnios) causing significant restriction of fetal movement. The fetal lungs are severely compressed and small for gestational age, highly concerning for primary pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal brain anatomy and ventricles are normal (atrium 6.1 mm) with age-appropriate early sulcation. Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis (Potter sequence) associated with severe anhydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

Cardiac MRI shows severe bi-leaflet prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium during systole, associated with a large eccentric regurgitant jet. The left atrium is severely dilated (LAVi 58 mL/m2). The left ventricle is moderately dilated (LVEDVi 112 mL/m2) with normal systolic function (LVEF 63%), representing chronic volume overload.

Impression: Severe mitral valve prolapse with severe mitral regurgitation and secondary left-sided chamber remodeling. Preserved left ventricular systolic function.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation reveals a severe brain malformation. There is partial separation of the cerebral hemispheres, with fusion of the frontal lobes and a single, monoventricle posteriorly that demonstrates rudimentary occipital horns. The interhemispheric fissure is present posteriorly but absent anteriorly. The thalami are partially fused. There is associated craniofacial dysmorphism, including hypotelorism and a flattened nasal bridge.

The posterior fossa appears intact. The remainder of the fetal body is unremarkable. Impression: Semilobar holoprosencephaly. Associated craniofacial anomalies are noted.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates marked global hypokinesia of the left ventricle with significant chamber dilation. The left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) is indexed at 115 mL/m2. Calculated left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is severely depressed at 32%. There is no evidence of focal myocardial edema or late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) to suggest myocardial infarction or acute myocarditis. Mild, non-specific right ventricular systolic dysfunction is also present with an RVEF of 45%.

Impression: Severe left ventricular dysfunction and ventricular dilation in a 32-year-old postpartum patient, highly characteristic of peripartum cardiomyopathy. No late gadolinium enhancement is noted, which represents a favorable prognostic indicator for potential functional recovery.

Fetal MRI at 30 weeks 4 days gestation. The corpus callosum is visualized but appears significantly thin and shortened, particularly in the posterior body and splenium, measuring only 15 mm in total length (below the 5th percentile). There is mild colpocephaly, with the posterior horns of the lateral ventricles measuring 9.5 mm. The anterior ventricles are normal. The remainder of the intracranial anatomy, including sulcation, is appropriate for 30 weeks.

The chest, abdomen, and spine are unremarkable. Impression: Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum with associated mild colpocephaly.

Fetal MRI at 34 weeks gestation demonstrates unremarkable intracranial and extracranial development. The cerebral cortex shows normal third-trimester sulcation, including well-demarcated central and cingulate sulci. The ventricular system is small and symmetric, measuring 5.7 mm at the atrium. The posterior fossa, corpus callosum, and orbits are entirely normal.

Fetal organs, including the cardiac, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal structures, are anatomically normal. Amniotic fluid volume is within normal limits. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating appropriate development of the central nervous system and body.

Fetal MRI at 20 weeks gestation demonstrates a lumbosacral myelomeningocele extending from L4 to S2 with a prominent defect in the overlying skin and subcutaneous tissue. Associated intracranial findings of Chiari II malformation are present, including a banana-shaped cerebellum, effacement of the cisterna magna, and a lemon-shaped skull. Lateral ventricles are dilated, with atrial measurements of 12.0 mm bilaterally.

Impression: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele with associated Chiari II malformation. Fetal surgery evaluation may be considered based on gestational age and anatomical criteria.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 30-year-old male with Tetralogy of Fallot status post surgical repair in infancy. There is severe right ventricular dilation (EDV index 165 mL/m2) and mild right ventricular dysfunction (RVEF 38%). High-resolution phase-contrast imaging reveals severe pulmonary regurgitation, with a calculated regurgitant fraction of 42% and severe dilation of the pulmonary trunk.

Impression: Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot presenting with severe chronic pulmonary regurgitation and secondary severe right ventricular dilation and dysfunction. Recommend valve replacement evaluation.

Fetal MRI at 21 weeks gestation demonstrates a lumbosacral myelomeningocele. There is a defect in the posterior element of the lower lumbar and sacral spine with herniation of a meningeal sac containing neural elements. Intracranial findings are highly characteristic of an associated Chiari II malformation, including a small posterior fossa, herniation of the cerebellar vermis through the foramen magnum (banana sign), and frontal bone scalloping (lemon sign). The lateral ventricles are dilated with the atrium measuring 10.8 mm. Cortical sulcation is appropriate for 21 weeks.

There is no evidence of additional visceral abnormalities. Impression: Open neural tube defect (lumbosacral myelomeningocele) with features of Chiari II malformation and mild ventriculomegaly. Maternal-fetal medicine consultation is recommended for surgical planning.

Cardiac MRI reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal diastolic wall thickness of 21 mm in the basal and mid-ventricular septum. There is systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve leading to dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and moderate mitral regurgitation. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging shows patchy mid-myocardial enhancement at the RV insertion points and within the hypertrophied septal segments.

Impression: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with significant asymmetric septal hypertrophy and associated LVOT obstruction. Left ventricular systolic function is hyperdynamic with an ejection fraction of 72%.

Cardiac MRI shows marked posterior displacement and systolic sagging of the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve, consistent with mitral valve prolapse (MVP). There is moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation, with a calculated regurgitant volume of 38 mL. The left atrium is moderately dilated, while the left ventricle demonstrates normal size and preserved systolic function, with an LVEF of 63%. No myocardial fibrosis is identified on LGE.

Impression: Mitral valve prolapse with moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation and associated moderate left atrial enlargement. Left ventricular size and systolic performance remain preserved.

Cardiac MRI performed to evaluate for suspected cardiac amyloidosis. Native T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) calculations are within the normal reference range. There is no evidence of diffuse or patchy late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Ventricular wall thicknesses, volumes, and overall systolic function are completely normal (LVEF 63%).

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. No evidence of infiltrative myocardial disease, cardiac amyloidosis, or focal fibrosis.

MRI of the brain demonstrates normal anatomical structure. The cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem are within normal limits without evidence of signal abnormalities, mass effect, or focal lesions. The ventricles and cortical sulci are appropriate in size for the patient's age. The major intracranial arterial flow voids are intact.

No evidence of restricted diffusion or acute ischemia. Impression: Normal brain MRI, showing no structural pathology to explain the patient's severe refractory headaches.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 31 weeks gestation demonstrates bilateral moderate ventriculomegaly. The lateral ventricles are symmetric but dilated, with the left atrium measuring 12.8 mm and the right atrium measuring 11.9 mm. There is no evidence of intraventricular hemorrhage or periventricular nodular heterotopia. The corpus callosum is fully formed. Cortical sulcation is appropriate for 31 weeks, showing expected development of the primary and secondary sulci.

The posterior fossa and remainder of the fetal visceral anatomy are within normal limits. Impression: Moderate bilateral fetal ventriculomegaly without associated intracranial anomalies. Close serial ultrasounds or follow-up MR are recommended.

Cardiac MRI shows a small perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) measuring 5 mm. There is a high-velocity left-to-right shunt across the defect with a calculated Qp:Qs ratio of 1.15. Left and right ventricular chamber sizes and wall thickness are within normal limits, and biventricular function is preserved (LVEF 62%).

Impression: Small, hemodynamically restrictive perimembranous VSD with a minor left-to-right shunt and no evidence of chambers remodeling or pulmonary hypertension.

Cardiac MRI shows marked dilation of the left ventricle (LVEDVI 142 mL/m2) and left atrium. There is global hypokinesis of the left ventricular free wall and septum, resulting in severe systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 24%. The right ventricle is also moderately dilated with mildly depressed function (RVEF 38%). Late gadolinium enhancement imaging reveals a narrow, patchy line of mid-wall enhancement in the basal interventricular septum, characteristic of non-ischemic etiology.

Impression: Severe non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with global biventricular hypokinesis and mid-wall myocardial fibrosis, indicating a poor prognostic substrate.

Brain MRI reveals an area of restricted diffusion with corresponding ADC hypointensity in the left frontal cortex and caudate nucleus, measuring approximately 3.2 cm in maximum dimension. This is associated with prominent T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, consistent with acute to subacute infarction in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory. No acute intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect is visualized.

Impression: Acute left MCA territory ischemic stroke. No hemorrhagic transformation is noted on susceptibility-weighted imaging.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate for suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy in a patient 4 weeks postpartum. The left ventricle is moderately dilated, with an end-diastolic volume index of 112 mL/m² and a significantly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) estimated at 32%. There is global hypokinesis of the left ventricular free wall, most pronounced at the apex. No regional wall motion abnormalities or areas of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) are identified, ruling out acute ischemic injury or focal myocardial scar.

Impression: Findings are highly consistent with peripartum cardiomyopathy. There is moderate left ventricular dysfunction and chamber dilatation. Close clinical monitoring and standard heart failure medical optimization are recommended.

MRI of the brain demonstrates hyperintense signal within the basal cisterns and right Sylvian fissure on FLAIR sequences, with corresponding signal loss on SWI, consistent with acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. No focal mass lesion is identified, but mild mass effect is noted on the adjacent temporal lobe. There is no evidence of ventricular enlargement at this time.

Impression: Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage centered within the basal cisterns and right Sylvian fissure. Urgent CT angiogram or conventional angiography is recommended to evaluate for an underlying ruptured aneurysm.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). The stomach, major parts of the left hepatic lobe, and several small bowel loops have herniated into the left hemithorax, causing a significant rightward mediastinal shift. The left lung is severely compressed and barely visualized, while the right lung volume appears moderately reduced for gestational age. Fetal brain MRI shows normal sulcation and ventricular measurements (atrium 6.2 mm).

Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver herniation and significant mediastinal shift. Fetal lung volume assessment is recommended to quantify pulmonary hypoplasia risk.

Sagittal T1-weighted sequences demonstrate herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 7 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. The tonsils appear pointed and peg-like. There is associated crowding of the craniocervical junction, but CSF flow is partially preserved. No evidence of cervical syringomyelia is seen on the upper spinal sequences.

Impression: Chiari I malformation. Tonsillar ectopia measures 7 mm with associated crowding at the level of the foramen magnum, correlating with clinical history of occipital headaches exacerbated by Valsalva.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation shows a normal, healthy fetus. Cortical development is unremarkable, demonstrating early Sylvian fissure formation and visible parieto-occipital sulcation appropriate for 24 weeks. The lateral ventricles are completely symmetrical and measure 5.9 mm. No spinal, abdominal, or cardiac structural abnormalities are detected.

Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating age-appropriate structural and central nervous system development.

Cardiac MRI performed for screening due to family history of sudden cardiac death. The study reveals completely normal cardiac anatomy. Left and right ventricular end-diastolic volumes and ejection fractions are within normal limits (LVEF 62%, RVEF 56%). There is no myocardial edema, regional wall motion abnormality, or late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI study. No imaging evidence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, or other structural pathologies associated with familial sudden cardiac death.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrates normal signal intensity and morphology of the cerebral hemispheres, brainstem, and cerebellum. The ventricular system, basal cisterns, and cerebral sulci are within normal limits for age. No abnormal extra-axial fluid collections or pathological enhancement are visualized following contrast administration.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain with no acute intracranial pathology or structural abnormalities identified. The study is completely normal, ruling out secondary causes for the patient's severe chronic headaches.

Brain MRI demonstrates normal intracranial anatomy for patient age. The basal ganglia and thalamus are symmetric and exhibit normal signal intensity on all sequences. There is no evidence of focal atrophy, mass lesion, acute ischemia, or hemorrhage. Ventricles and sulci are within normal limits.

Impression: Normal MRI of the brain. No structural basal ganglia or brainstem lesions identified to account for the patient's resting tremor.

Brain MR imaging demonstrates normal intracranial structures with preserved gray-white matter differentiation. The ventricles, sulci, and cisterns are within normal limits. There is no evidence of ischemia, hemorrhage, mass effect, or pathological contrast enhancement. Visualized paranasal sinuses are clear.

Impression: Normal MR of the brain. No structural or vascular pathology identified to account for the patient's recurrent syncope episodes.

Cardiac MRI was requested for the workup of frequent PVCs in an otherwise healthy 32-year-old female. Cine images demonstrate normal left and right ventricular chamber sizes, wall thickness, and global function. Calculated LVEF is 61% and RVEF is 57% with no regional wall motion abnormalities or aneurysm formation. No late gadolinium enhancement is noted to suggest scar or fibrosis.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. There is no evidence of structural heart disease, arrhythmogenic substrates, or myocardial scarring to explain the patient's ventricular ectopy.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation demonstrates a normal examination. Fetal brain tissue shows normal signal intensity without evidence of ischemic injury or hemorrhage. The lateral ventricles are within normal parameters, with an atrial width of 5.9 mm. Early sulcal lines match expected landmarks for 24 weeks gestation.

The spine, cardiac silhouette, lungs, and stomach are all normally positioned and formed. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study at 24 weeks gestation showing age-appropriate structural and neuro-developmental progression.

Brain MRI demonstrates herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 7.5 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. The tonsils are pointed (peg-like) in morphology. There is associated crowding of the craniocervical junction. Cervical spine screening sequences demonstrate no evidence of syringomyelia.

Impression: Chiari I malformation. No associated syrinx seen on scout images of the cervical spine, but clinical correlation for suboccipital headaches is suggested.

High-resolution multiplanar MR imaging of the brain and orbits demonstrates symmetric cerebral hemispheres with unremarkable gray-white matter differentiation. The optic nerves, chiasm, and optic tracts are normal in caliber and signal intensity. The ventricular system, basal cisterns, and major vascular flow voids are entirely normal.

Impression: Normal MRI of the brain and orbits. No structural anomaly, mass, or demyelinating process is identified along the visual pathways.

Fetal MRI at 34 weeks gestation demonstrates a left-sided diaphragmatic hernia. The stomach and small bowel loops are herniated into the left chest, resulting in a moderate mediastinal shift to the right. The left lung is compressed and its volume is severely reduced. The right lung appears normal. Fetal brain maturation and sulcation are appropriate for 34 weeks, and lateral ventricles are symmetric at 5.8 mm.

No other anomalies are identified. Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with severe compression of the left lung.

Brain MRI obtained for evaluation of unilateral left-sided tinnitus. There is no evidence of CPA mass, particularly no vestibular schwannoma or meningioma. Internal auditory canals are symmetric and normal in appearance. The brain parenchyma is free of mass, acute infarction, or hemorrhage. The ventricles and cerebral sulci are normal.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals, with no CPA lesions, acute intracranial process, or structural correlates for left-sided tinnitus.

Fetal MRI at 30 weeks gestation demonstrates age-appropriate fetal brain maturation. Sulcation and gyration of the cerebral cortex are normal for 30 weeks, displaying clear parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci. The lateral ventricles are symmetric and within normal limits, measuring 5.9 mm at the atrium. The corpus callosum and posterior fossa elements are well-visualized and structurally intact.

Fetal chest, abdomen, and limbs are normal without any structural anomalies. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study showing age-appropriate brain sulcal development and normal anatomy.

MR of the brain demonstrates a large, heterogeneously enhancing mass with a central necrotic core in the right frontoparietal lobe, measuring 4.8 x 4.2 x 3.9 cm. There is extensive surrounding vasogenic edema resulting in a 7 mm leftward midline shift and partial compression of the right lateral ventricle.

Impression: Highly aggressive intra-axial neoplasm, diagnostic of glioblastoma multiforme. Neurosurgical oncology consultation should be initiated immediately.

Cardiac MRI of a 45-year-old male with atypical chest pain and an equivocal stress test. The left and right ventricular chamber sizes and wall thicknesses are normal. Global systolic function is preserved with an LVEF of 60% and RVEF of 54%. Multiplanar cine imaging shows no regional wall motion abnormalities. First-pass perfusion imaging under resting conditions demonstrates normal, homogeneous myocardial perfusion without inducible perfusion defects. Late gadolinium enhancement is completely absent.

Impression: Unremarkable cardiac MRI. Normal ventricular function and myocardial perfusion with no evidence of myocardial ischemia or prior infarction.

MRI of the brain demonstrates a crescentic, extra-axial fluid collection along the right frontoparietal convexity measuring 1.2 cm in maximal thickness. The collection exhibits heterogeneous signal intensity on both T1 and T2 sequences, consistent with a chronic subdural hematoma with acute-on-chronic hemorrhagic components. There is moderate compression of the right lateral ventricle and a 4 mm leftward midline shift.

Impression: Subacute to chronic right frontoparietal subdural hematoma with evidence of recent re-bleeding, causing moderate mass effect and midline shift.

MRI demonstrates a well-demarcated, extra-axial mass arising from the right parasagittal dura. The mass measures 2.8 x 2.4 x 2.1 cm and shows homogeneous, intense contrast enhancement with a prominent dural tail. There is mild mass effect on the adjacent postcentral gyrus, accompanied by a small amount of surrounding vasogenic edema in the adjacent white matter.

Impression: Extra-axial mass arising from the right parasagittal dura, highly consistent with a benign meningioma. Mild surrounding edema and mass effect are present.

Fetal MRI at 34 weeks 6 days gestation demonstrates a right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The right hemidiaphragm is deficient, with herniation of the right lobe of the liver and a loop of small bowel into the right hemithorax. There is a leftward mediastinal shift with significant compression of both lungs. The left lung is compressed against the left chest wall. Calculated total fetal lung volume is reduced at approximately 52% of predicted value for gestational age.

No associated intracranial abnormalities are noted, and the brain shows normal sulcation for 34 weeks. Impression: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver herniation and severe pulmonary hypoplasia.

Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and MRI of the brain demonstrate a well-defined saccular outpouching arising from the ophthalmic segment of the left internal carotid artery. The aneurysm measures approximately 5.2 x 4.8 mm with a neck measuring 3.1 mm. There is no surrounding edema or parenchymal signaling abnormality to suggest acute rupture.

Impression: Small saccular aneurysm of the left internal carotid artery (ophthalmic segment), unruptured. No associated acute cerebral ischemia or hemorrhage.

MRI of the brain reveals acute subarachnoid hemorrhage, localized primarily within the suprasellar cistern and bilateral Sylvian fissures. MR angiography (MRA) demonstrates a 6 mm saccular aneurysm arising from the anterior communicating artery. Mild early ventricular dilatation suggests early communicating hydrocephalus.

Impression: Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage secondary to a ruptured 6 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Urgent neurosurgical intervention is indicated.

Brain MRI performed for evaluation of vertigo demonstrates normal signal intensity and morphology of the brainstem, cerebellum, and CPA cisterns. No acute infarctions or hemorrhages are present. The ventricles and extra-axial spaces are appropriate in size for the patient's age. The major intracranial flow voids are intact.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. No central structural etiology identified to account for the patient's dizziness or vertigo.

Brain MR imaging shows a broad-based, extra-axial, intensely and homogeneously enhancing mass measuring 2.5 x 2.2 cm along the left sphenoid wing. There is a prominent 'dural tail' sign and mild localized mass effect on the adjacent left temporal lobe. No significant surrounding edema or invasion of the cavernous sinus is visualized.

Impression: Extra-axial enhancing mass along the left sphenoid wing, characteristic of a benign meningioma. Clinical follow-up or neurosurgical consultation is recommended based on symptoms.

Brain MRI of a patient with a history of metastatic breast cancer reveals three discrete, well-circumscribed, ring-enhancing lesions. The largest lesion is located in the left cerebellar hemisphere (1.5 cm) with surrounding vasogenic edema. Two smaller lesions are identified at the gray-white junction of the right frontal and left temporal lobes (each measuring < 8 mm).

Impression: Multiple enhancing intracranial lesions, highly consistent with cerebral metastases in this clinical context. Associated mass effect and edema are most prominent in the left cerebellum.

Cardiac MRI shows normal left and right ventricular dimensions. The myocardial wall thickness is within physiological limits throughout. The left ventricular ejection fraction is normal at 61%, and the right ventricular ejection fraction is 58%. There is no evidence of resting myocardial perfusion defects or late gadolinium enhancement to suggest myocardial scar or fibrosis.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI with preserved biventricular systolic function. No evidence of myocardial infarction, structural cardiomyopathy, or valvular heart disease.

Brain MRI reveals a large area of restricted diffusion involving the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, demonstrating hyperintensity on DWI and corresponding hypointensity on ADC mapping. Associated swelling of the cortical gyri and effacement of the adjacent sulci is noted. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the circle of Willis demonstrates abrupt cutoff of the right MCA M1 segment.

Impression: Acute ischemic infarction within the right middle cerebral artery territory secondary to M1 segment occlusion. Significant mass effect on adjacent sulci without midline shift at this time.

Fetal MRI at 33 weeks gestation reveals a malformation of cortical development. There is severe, localized thickening and irregular nodularity of the bilateral perisylvian cortex, suggestive of polymicrogyria or opercular dysplasia. The sylvian fissures are abnormally wide and vertically oriented. Moderate bilateral ventriculomegaly is noted, with the left atrium measuring 11.5 mm and the right atrium measuring 10.8 mm.

The corpus callosum is intact but thin. The posterior fossa is normal. Impression: Cortical malformation consistent with bilateral polymicrogyria, associated with moderate ventriculomegaly and delayed opercularization.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed using multiplanar, multisequence protocols. The brain parenchyma is unremarkable, showing normal gray-white matter differentiation and no focal lesions or signal abnormalities. Ventricles, sulci, and cisterns are normal in size and appearance, and no acute hemorrhage or infarct is visualized.

Impression: Unremarkable MRI of the brain. No structural, ischemic, or neoplastic pathology identified.

MRI of the internal auditory canals and brain reveals a lobulated, enhancing mass in the left cerebellopontine angle measuring 1.4 x 1.2 cm. The mass extends into and mildly widens the left internal auditory canal. It demonstrates intermediate signal on T1 and heterogeneous hyperintensity on T2. There is mild mass effect on the adjacent cerebellar hemisphere.

Impression: Left vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) with intracanalicular and cisternal components. Recommend ENT and neurosurgical consultation.

Fetal MRI at 23 weeks gestation demonstrates a large lumbosacral myelomeningocele with associated Chiari II malformation. There is a defect in the distal spinal canal with herniation of meninges and neural elements into an external sac measuring 2.4 x 1.8 cm. Intracranially, there is a classic 'banana sign' of the cerebellum and 'lemon sign' of the calvarium. The lateral ventricles show colpocephaly with the left atrium measuring 12.4 mm and the right measuring 11.8 mm.

Cortical sulcation is slightly delayed for 23 weeks, with shallow sylvian fissures. Impression: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele with classic Chiari II malformation features, including mild ventriculomegaly and delayed opercularization.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation reveals complete agenesis of the corpus callosum. There is characteristic colpocephaly with dilated, teardrop-shaped posterior horns of the lateral ventricles measuring 13.2 mm on the left and 12.8 mm on the right, while the frontal horns are narrow and widely spaced. The third ventricle is elevated and moderately dilated. Probst bundles are visualized running parallel to the interhemispheric fissure.

The gyral pattern along the medial hemispheric surface demonstrates a radial arrangement pointing toward the third ventricle. No other intracranial abnormalities are seen. Impression: Complete agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated colpocephaly and characteristic radial gyral pattern.

MRI reveals a well-demarcated, extra-axial mass along the left frontal convexity measuring 3.2 x 2.8 x 2.5 cm. The lesion is dural-based, shows uniform, intense contrast enhancement, and demonstrates a prominent 'dural tail' sign. There is mild compression of the adjacent cerebral cortex and minimal surrounding vasogenic edema.

Impression: Features are consistent with a benign left frontal convexity meningioma. Mass effect on the brain parenchyma is minimal with no midline shift.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation reveals a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Multiple loops of bowel, the stomach, and a portion of the left lobe of the liver are herniated into the left hemithorax. This has resulted in a significant rightward mediastinal shift and compression of the fetal heart. The right lung appears compressed but is visualized, while the left lung volume is severely diminished. Fetal brain assessment shows normal development with appropriate sulcation patterns for 31 weeks and normal lateral ventricles (atrial width 5.4 mm).

Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic hernia of stomach, bowel, and liver, leading to significant mediastinal shift and pulmonary hypoplasia.

Cardiac MRI reveals marked thickening and redundancy of both the anterior and posterior mitral valve leaflets (Barlow's disease pathology) with prominent systolic prolapse of both leaflets into the left atrium. There is a large, eccentric regurgitant jet visible on cine sequences, consistent with severe mitral regurgitation. The left atrium is severely dilated, and the left ventricle is moderately dilated (LVEDVI 110 mL/m2) with a hyperdynamic ejection fraction of 65%.

Impression: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to bileaflet mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous mitral valve disease), with associated severe left atrial enlargement and early left ventricular dilatation.

Fetal MRI at 20 weeks gestation performed for family history of congenital heart disease. The study demonstrates normal early fetal brain development. The cerebral cortex is smooth, which is normal for this early gestational age, and the lateral ventricular atria are symmetric and measure 5.2 mm. The corpus callosum is developing normally. The cerebellum, vermis, and brainstem appear normal.

The fetal heart, visceral organs, and spinal cord are grossly normal. Impression: Normal fetal MRI at 20 weeks gestation. No intracranial, spinal, or visceral malformations are identified.

Fetal MRI performed at 27 weeks gestation demonstrates a large defect in the left hemidiaphragm. There is herniation of the stomach, several loops of small bowel, and a portion of the left hepatic lobe into the left hemithorax. This has resulted in a significant rightward mediastinal shift, with severe compression of both the left and right lungs. The fetal lung-to-head ratio (LHR) is estimated at 1.05, indicating significant pulmonary hypoplasia risk. The fetal brain MRI demonstrates normal intracranial anatomy with symmetric lateral ventricles measuring 5.2 mm.

Fetal spinal alignment and abdominal viscera are otherwise unremarkable. Impression: Large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) containing stomach, bowel, and left hepatic lobe, resulting in severe mediastinal shift and pulmonary hypoplasia.

Cardiac MRI shows patchy subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) localized to the basal-to-mid lateral and inferolateral walls. T2-weighted triple-inversion recovery imaging demonstrates corresponding hyperintensity, indicating active myocardial edema. Left ventricular systolic function is borderline reduced at 49% with mild hypokinesis of the lateral wall. The right ventricular size and function are within normal limits.

Impression: Clinical and MRI findings satisfy the updated Lake Louise Criteria for acute myocarditis, with localized subepicardial injury and myocardial edema. Left ventricular systolic function is borderline reduced.

Fetal MRI at 34 weeks gestation demonstrates a right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The liver is herniated into the right chest cavity, causing significant leftward shift of the mediastinum and compressing the left lung. Total fetal lung volume is severely reduced, measured at approximately 18 mL. The fetal brain is normal with a ventricular atrium of 5.4 mm.

Impression: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic liver herniation and severe pulmonary hypoplasia. High risk for neonatal respiratory distress.

High-resolution cine sequences identify a small muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD) in the mid-muscular septum measuring approximately 4 mm. Phase-contrast flow analysis demonstrates a tiny left-to-right shunt with a calculated Qp:Qs ratio of 1.2. The left and right ventricular chambers show completely normal sizes and volumes with preserved global ejection fractions (LVEF 61%).

Impression: Small, hemodynamically insignificant muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD) with a minor left-to-right shunt. No evidence of right heart strain or volume overload is identified.

Fetal MRI performed at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates a large left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). The stomach, major portion of the small bowel loops, and a small segment of the left hepatic lobe are herniated into the left hemithorax. This exerts significant mass effect, with severe rightward mediastinal shift and compression of the right lung. The observed-to-expected total lung volume is severely decreased, estimated at approximately 28%.

Fetal brain anatomy and ventricles are normal, with an atrial width of 6.2 mm and normal sulcation. Impression: Left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with significant herniation of abdominal viscera, mediastinal shift, and severe secondary pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks 1 day gestation reveals complete absence of the corpus callosum. The lateral ventricles show a characteristic colpocephalic configuration, with narrow frontal horns and dilated posterior horns measuring 12.5 mm on the left and 12.8 mm on the right. There is widening of the interhemispheric fissure and radial alignment of the medial sulci (steer-horn configuration of the frontal horns on coronal view). The third ventricle is superiorly displaced.

The posterior fossa, cerebellum, and brainstem are otherwise normal. The fetal chest and abdomen are unremarkable. Impression: Complete agenesis of the corpus callosum associated with bilateral colpocephaly.

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks gestation shows marked, bilateral lateral ventriculomegaly. The left atrial diameter measures 16.5 mm and the right measures 15.8 mm. There is thinning of the cerebral cortex and prominent dangling of the choroid plexuses within both ventricles. The third ventricle is minimally dilated. The corpus callosum and posterior fossa structures are present but compressed.

The remainder of the fetal structures, including the spine, chest, and abdomen, are normal in appearance. Impression: Severe bilateral fetal ventriculomegaly. Close monitoring and pediatric neurosurgical planning are recommended.

Cardiac MRI was requested to evaluate atypical, non-exertional chest pain in a 48-year-old female. Multiplanar, multisequence imaging demonstrates completely normal cardiac architecture. Biventricular chamber sizes are within normal limits, and there are no regional or global wall motion abnormalities. The left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 65%. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging is completely negative for focal scar or fibrosis.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI. No evidence of myocardial infarction, active myocarditis, or structural heart disease.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal biventricular dimensions, wall thickness, and mass index. The left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 65% and the right ventricular ejection fraction is 58%, without any detectable wall motion abnormalities. Valvular structures are normal in appearance and show no evidence of stenosis or regurgitation.

T1 mapping and late gadolinium enhancement sequences are negative for myocardial edema, infiltration, or scar tissue. Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI study showing preserved biventricular systolic function and no evidence of myocardial pathology.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation reveals severe micromelia involving all limbs. The long bones of the upper and lower extremities are markedly shortened, thickened, and slightly bowed, particularly the femora and humeri. The thorax is narrow and bell-shaped, indicating pulmonary hypoplasia. The head is relatively large with prominent frontal bossing.

The fetal brain is structurally intact with normal ventricular measurements (atrium 6.1 mm) and appropriate early sulcation. Impression: Skeletal dysplasia, highly characteristic of thanatophoric dysplasia or severe osteogenesis imperfecta. Genetic counseling and pediatric palliative care consultation are recommended.

Cardiac MRI was requested as a baseline assessment of cardiac function before the initiation of cardiotoxic chemotherapy for newly diagnosed breast cancer. The left and right ventricles are normal in size, and biventricular systolic function is normal. The left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 63%. There are no regional wall motion abnormalities, myocardial edema, or late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI. Preserved global biventricular function provides a reassuring baseline for the planned chemotherapy regimen.

Brain MRI with contrast reveals diffuse, smooth, non-nodular pachymeningeal (dural) enhancement. There is mild sagging of the brainstem, inferior displacement of the cerebellar tonsils (2 mm), and mild enlargement of the pituitary gland, giving it a prominent, 'plump' appearance.

Impression: MRI findings strongly suggestive of intracranial hypotension, characteristic of a spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. Suggest correlation with clinical history of severe orthostatic headaches.

Cardiac MRI reveals significant dilatation of the right atrium and right ventricle. The right ventricular end-diastolic volume index is elevated at 135 mL/m2, with moderate right ventricular volume overload. A large defect in the mid-atrial septum is visualized, measuring approximately 18 mm, with clear left-to-right shunting demonstrated on phase-contrast velocity mapping. The Qp:Qs shunt ratio is calculated at 1.8.

Impression: Large ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) resulting in moderate right heart dilatation and volume overload. Left ventricular size and systolic function (EF 60%) remain normal.

A comprehensive cardiac MRI study was completed using standard cine and perfusion imaging protocols. Left and right ventricular chamber dimensions are within normal limits for body surface area. Left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 64%, and right ventricular ejection fraction is 59%, with no focal wall motion abnormalities or areas of dyskinesis. Myocardial perfusion is uniform during stress, and late gadolinium enhancement shows no focal fibrosis.

Impression: Unremarkable cardiac MRI. Normal ventricular volumes, preserved global and regional systolic functions, and no evidence of myocardial ischemia or structural fibrosis.

Cardiac and aortic MRI demonstrates a localized narrowing of the descending thoracic aorta immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, measuring 9 mm in internal diameter, consistent with aortic coarctation. Significant collateral vascular channels are noted, particularly arising from the internal mammary and intercostal arteries. There is a secondary concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (septal wall thickness 14 mm) due to chronic afterload elevation.

Left ventricular systolic function is preserved with an ejection fraction of 64%. No significant aortic valve stenosis or regurgitation is identified. Impression: Coarctation of the thoracic aorta with prominent collateral circulation and compensatory left ventricular concentric hypertrophy. No acute aortic dissection is present.

Brain MRI was performed on a 29-year-old female patient, currently at 34 weeks gestation, presenting with sudden-onset seizures and severe hypertension. MR sequences demonstrate focal, patchy, and symmetric areas of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity within the cortical and subcortical white matter of the bilateral parieto-occipital regions. There is no evidence of diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC mapping to suggest acute infarction, and no intracranial hemorrhage is identified.

Impression: Imaging findings are highly characteristic of Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES), occurring in the clinical context of preeclampsia/eclampsia. Close clinical monitoring and blood pressure management are recommended, with follow-up imaging to confirm resolution.

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrates an area of restricted diffusion with corresponding low ADC values within the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, specifically involving the left insular cortex and frontoparietal operculum. Minimal mass effect is observed, with no midline shift. No intracranial hemorrhage is identified on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI).

Impression: Acute ischemic stroke within the left MCA territory. No hemorrhagic transformation is visualized on current sequences. Prompt clinical management is recommended.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates an atypical posterior fossa morphology. The cerebellar vermis is hypoplastic and rotated upwards, and there is mild enlargement of the cisterna magna, which communicates with the fourth ventricle. However, the torcular is not significantly elevated, consistent with a Dandy-Walker variant. Symmetrical ventriculomegaly is noted with atrial widths of 11.5 mm.

Cortical gyration patterns and tertiary sulcation are appropriate for 35 weeks. The fetal chest and limbs are within normal limits. Impression: Dandy-Walker variant with hypoplastic cerebellar vermis and mild bilateral ventriculomegaly.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks 5 days gestation reveals moderate bilateral ventriculomegaly. The lateral ventricular atria measure 12.8 mm on the right and 12.4 mm on the left. The third ventricle is minimally dilated at 2.8 mm. There is thinning of the corpus callosum, though it is fully formed. The cerebral sulcation and gyration are slightly delayed but generally within acceptable limits for 31 weeks.

No other structural abnormalities of the brain are identified. The fetal chest, abdomen, and spine are normal. Impression: Moderate bilateral ventriculomegaly without associated intracranial anomalies. Recommend serial follow-up.

Cardiac MRI reveals marked dilation of the right ventricle with global and regional wall abnormalities, including dyskinesia of the right ventricular outflow tract and inferior wall. The right ventricular end-diastolic volume index is severely increased at 135 mL/m2, and the RVEF is depressed at 31%. LGE imaging shows focal fibrofatty replacement in the RV free wall and RVOT. Left ventricular size and function are normal (LVEF 58%).

Impression: Severe right ventricular dilation and dysfunction with characteristic regional abnormalities and LGE, meeting the diagnostic Task Force Criteria for Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC).

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks gestation demonstrates partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior aspect (rostrum and genu) of the corpus callosum is formed, but the body and posterior splenium are absent. The third ventricle is elevated. Mild colpocephaly is noted, with the posterior horns measuring 11.2 mm at the atrium. Sulcation is characterized by slight distortion of the medial hemispheric sulci, showing radial gyration posteriorly, consistent with the partial callosal defect.

The posterior fossa, spine, and visceral organs are structurally normal. Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated mild posterior ventriculomegaly/colpocephaly. Recommend pediatric neurosurgical consultation.

MRI of the brain demonstrates flattening of the posterior sclera bilaterally, prominent CSF space surrounding the optic nerves, and mild empty sella turcica. There is also bilateral, symmetric transverse venous sinus stenosis noted on the 3D MR venogram sequences. No space-occupying lesions or hydrocephalus are present.
